chef_bio.background: apelila is a 100% plant-based bakery and café tucked into the Takano neighborhood of Sakyo Ward, a short walk from Demachiyanagi station and Shimogamo Shrine, sitting along the river on Kawabata-dori. It was opened in 2015 by owner-baker Takahashi Sayaka, who had previously taught bread-making classes before turning her craft into a shop offering more than 20 kinds of bread.
chef_bio.philosophy: Takahashi-san is reportedly not vegan herself; she chooses to bake entirely without animal-derived ingredients because she wants people to discover how delicious naturally-fermented yeast and simple, well-sourced ingredients can be. The shop leans on sustainability and quality: in-house milled Kyoto-grown whole wheat, organic dried fruit, and a decades-old starter.
chef_bio.specialty: Naturally-leavened vegan breads and baked goods made with a house-milled Kyoto whole-wheat flour and a sourdough starter that has been continuously fed for roughly two decades; plus a café lunch headlined by a vegan cheeseburger plate with a chickpea patty and fermented soy yogurt, alongside donuts, melon bread, caramel cream pastries, cookies and waffles.

anecdotes.text: The bread is built on a natural sourdough starter that has been continuously fed and kept alive for roughly 19–20 years, paired with whole-wheat flour milled in-house from Kyoto-grown grain.
Takahashi Sayaka opened apelila in 2015 after previously running bread-making classes, and keeps animal ingredients out of her bread to let customers taste the umami of fermentation.
The café has a calming atmosphere with a small zen garden and a back seating area where diners remove their shoes.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: orangepage confirms the ~20-year continuously-fed natural starter and in-house-milled Kyoto whole wheat at this Takano/Sakyo-Ward vegan bakery; LEE names owner Takahashi Sayaka, her 2015 opening, prior bread-making classes and her focus on fermentation's umami.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat is everywhere: this is a whole-wheat bakery with house-milled flour, so flour dust and gluten cross-contact are unavoidable throughout the kitchen. Not safe for celiacs.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Entirely plant-based kitchen with no butter, eggs, or dairy used in any product, so there is no animal cross-contact to worry about.

staff_allergy_handling.text: English is limited and menu labels are mostly Japanese, but staff are reportedly eager to help answer ingredient questions.

positives.text: 100% vegan bakery and café — every bread, baked good, and lunch item is plant-based, so vegans can order anything on the menu with confidence.
Uses soy-based cream and plant milks plus fermented soy yogurt in place of all dairy.

cultural_comfort.note: Menus and labels are mostly in Japanese with limited English, but staff are reportedly eager to help with ingredient questions, so a few Japanese phrases will smooth your visit.

vm_mamezen_tonyu_ramen_senm.gf_detail: Not a dedicated GF kitchen, but genuinely GF-aware: gluten-free rice noodles are available as a swap (+250 yen), and the official menu states a wheat-free soy sauce is used when the rice noodles are selected. Standard ramen noodles contain wheat. The kitchen uses a single boiling pot but separate preparation can be requested, so a celiac should explicitly ask for the rice-noodle/wheat-free-soy preparation and confirm separate cooking.
vm_mamezen_tonyu_ramen_senm.vegan_detail: Everything served is 100% vegan, no animal products at all. Since 2014 the kitchen follows an "Oriental Vegan" approach rooted in shojin (Buddhist temple) cuisine, excluding eggs, fish stock, the five pungent alliums (no green onion/garlic/onion), and using no fish dashi. Signature dishes are the Musashi soy-milk ramen (yuba/tofu skin, mizuna, pickled plum, yuzu, sansho mushrooms, seaweed) and a soybean-meat tantan ramen.
vm_mamezen_tonyu_ramen_senm.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan/vegetarian] MameZen (also styled TowZen) opened on July 26, 2004 in Kyoto's Shimogamo district as a hidden, speakeasy-style soy-milk ramen house. Its founder, Minoru Yonekawa, spent about ten years managing a Kyoto tofu restaurant before reframing his cooking as food heal

chef_bio.background: MameZen (also styled TowZen) opened on July 26, 2004 in Kyoto's Shimogamo district as a hidden, speakeasy-style soy-milk ramen house. Its founder, Minoru Yonekawa, spent about ten years managing a Kyoto tofu restaurant before reframing his cooking as food healing cuisine.
chef_bio.philosophy: Completely animal-free cooking grounded in Zen shojin-ryori principles, avoiding the five pungent alliums, and pursuing the healing that food brings, framing veganism as kinder to health and environment.
chef_bio.specialty: Soy-milk-based ramen, the signature Musashi bowl topped with yuba, mizuna, pickled plum, yuzu, seaweed and sansho mushrooms, plus a soybean-meat tantan ramen; vegan sushi by advance reservation.

anecdotes.text: Began as a hidden retreat pairing soy-milk ramen with flute performances and Zenbient meditation, transitioning around 2009 into a community gathering space.
Went fully 100% vegan on January 1, 2014, removing eggs, fish stock and onions; celebrated its 20th anniversary in July 2024.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: mamezen.com's About page states founder Minoru Yonekawa managed a Kyoto tofu restaurant ~10 years before opening TowZen on 2004/7/26 as a hidden retreat with flute/Zenbient events, opened up around April 2009, and went fully vegan on 2014/1/1 (removing eggs, onions and fish broth).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Kitchen uses a single boiling pot, but separate preparation is available on request, important for a celiac ordering gluten-free rice noodles alongside wheat ramen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: A wheat-free soy sauce is used when the gluten-free rice noodles are selected; standard ramen uses wheat noodles.
soy_sauce_wheat.source_wording: イチビキのグルテンフリー醤油を使用し、米粉麺（グルテンフリー麺）を選べばほぼグルテンフリーですが…

vegan_cross_contact.text: Kitchen is 100% vegan with no animal products on premises, so there is no meat, fish or dairy cross-contact.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Menu explicitly offers gluten-free rice noodles and notes separate preparation can be requested.

positives.text: Fully vegan, animal-free kitchen rooted in shojin cuisine, no fish dashi, eggs or dairy anywhere, very low-risk for vegan travelers.
Offers a genuine gluten-free path (rice noodles plus wheat-free soy sauce), uncommon for a ramen shop.
positives.source_wording: イチビキのグルテンフリー醤油を使用し、米粉麺（グルテンフリー麺）を選べばほぼグルテンフリーですが、普通の小麦の麺と茹で窯は同じものを使用しておりますので、極々微量の小麦が含まれる可能性があります。

cultural_comfort.note: The restaurant maintains a full English website and English menu and is well-known among foreign vegan travelers, so an English-speaking student should feel comfortable here.

vm_kissa_hobodo_cafe_hobodo.gf_detail: No gluten-free claim is made by the cafe and none of the sources document GF accommodation. The menu includes clearly wheat-containing items (homemade flatbread, spring rolls/gyoza wrappers, falafel, sweets) and Japanese set meals typically use standard miso and soy sauce, which usually contain wheat. Brown-rice and rice-based dishes (e.g. edamame rice, some ohagi) may be naturally gluten-free, but no dedicated GF preparation or wheat-free soy sauce is confirmed. A gluten-sensitive diner should ask in person about each dish; the staff speak some English.
vm_kissa_hobodo_cafe_hobodo.vegan_detail: A fully plant-based (vegan) cafe and bookshop. Multiple sources confirm everything on the menu is vegan ("全てヴィーガンOK") - no meat, fish, dairy, eggs or honey. The owner's wife, who runs the kitchen, follows a plant-based lifestyle and the cafe was founded so "everyone can eat together without worry." Food centers on seasonal vegetables sourced from local organic/natural farms: a daily set meal (brown or edamame rice, miso soup, and several vegetable side dishes), plus dishes like vegetable-and-bean curry, pumpkin-carrot soup, spring rolls/gyoza, falafel, and six varieties of brown-rice ohagi (sweet rice cakes). Because the kitchen is entirely vegan, there is no animal-protein cross-contact.
vm_kissa_hobodo_cafe_hobodo.hours_raw: Fri-Sun, doors from 10:00, food service 11:00/11:30-17:00 (last order ~16:30). Closed Mon-Thu. Also closes irregularly on some open days - check Instagram (@hobodocafe) for the monthly schedule.
vm_kissa_hobodo_cafe_hobodo.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan/vegetarian] Hobodo is a tiny vegan cafe-and-bookshop run by a husband-and-wife team, Daijiro and Misayo Satoh, who opened it in spring 2016. Daijiro handles the coffee (using beans from a local Kyoto roaster, with Italian Blend and Panama varieties), while Misayo, who liv

chef_bio.background: Hobodo is a tiny vegan cafe-and-bookshop run by a husband-and-wife team, Daijiro and Misayo Satoh, who opened it in 2014. Daijiro handles the coffee (using beans from a local Kyoto roaster, Cafe de Corazon, with an Italian Blend and Panama variety), while Misayo, who lives a plant-based lifestyle, cooks the food. The couple deliberately keep the place small, book-filled and open only a few days a week so guests can linger and read while they eat.
chef_bio.philosophy: They named the cafe after early-20th-century American 'hobos,' embracing a free, independent spirit. The kitchen is entirely plant-based so that, in their words, everyone can sit down and eat together without worry; they prioritize seasonal vegetables from local organic and natural farms and balance the shop around family life.
chef_bio.specialty: A daily-changing vegetable set meal (brown or edamame rice, miso soup and several seasonal vegetable side dishes), plus several kinds of brown-rice ohagi in unusual flavors (egoma/perilla, rum-raisin, hazelnut, roasted-tea and more), spring rolls, falafel and homemade flatbread.

anecdotes.text: The couple chose the name 'Hobodo' in homage to American hobos of the early 1900s, embracing that wandering, independent spirit for their homey DIY cafe.
Misayo creates a fully vegan menu specifically so that 'everyone can eat together without concern,' sourcing produce directly from organic and naturally-cultivated farms.

Their weekly-changing brown-rice-and-seasonal-vegetable bento is popular as a takeaway to carry to the rooftop terrace of the Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art (the 'Higashiyama Cube'), a short walk away.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: karafuneya and other Kyoto listings say the Satoh couple opened Hobodo in 2014, open only a few days a week; Daijiro sources beans from roaster Cafe de Corazon; the name honors early-1900s American hobos; crea.bunshun recommends buying its brown-rice/vegetable bento to eat at the nearby Kyocera Museum rooftop terrace.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No gluten-free protocol is documented; wheat-based items (homemade flatbread, gyoza/spring-roll wrappers, falafel, sweets) are prepared in the same small kitchen, so cross-contact with wheat should be assumed unless confirmed in person.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Set meals include miso soup and seasoned vegetable dishes; no source confirms wheat-free tamari is used, so standard wheat-containing soy sauce and miso should be assumed.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The entire kitchen is plant-based, so there is no risk of cross-contact with meat, fish, dairy, eggs or honey - every item served is vegan.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The owner-couple speak some English and provide an English menu, making it feasible to ask about ingredients; no formal allergen protocol is documented, so confirm specific needs directly with them.

positives.text: 100% vegan cafe and bookshop - all menu items are confirmed vegan, eliminating animal-product cross-contact concerns.
Produce is sourced from local organic and naturally-cultivated farms, and the menu is built around fresh seasonal vegetables.

cultural_comfort.note: The friendly couple who run it speak some English and have an English menu, so a foreign student can manage comfortably with just a little Japanese.

vm_seigen_in_saigen_in.gf_detail: No gluten-free information is published. The core dish is tofu, vegetables and the seven herbs of yudofu, which can be naturally GF, but the dipping sauce and any soy sauce / seasonings are an unknown gluten risk (typical Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and the dipping sauce is reportedly fish-based and otherwise unspecified). The shojin set may include other components. A gluten-sensitive diner must ask directly about the sauce, soy sauce and condiments; staff speak only limited English, so a written allergy card in Japanese is advisable.
vm_seigen_in_saigen_in.vegan_detail: Seigen-in serves a seven-herb yudofu (hot tofu pot, ~2,000 yen) and a shojin ryori (Buddhist vegetarian) set with tofu pot (~4,000 yen). The food itself is plant-based tofu-and-vegetable temple fare, so the bulk of the meal is suitable for vegetarians and largely for vegans. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: multiple HappyCow reviewers report that the dipping sauce served with the yudofu is fish-based (not vegan) — so despite the VegeMap "all-vegan" tag, a strict vegan should explicitly decline the dipping sauce and ask what condiments contain. As a temple-style (shojin) kitchen it should avoid meat, but vegans cannot assume the dashi/sauce is plant-based and must ask. Best treated as vegetarian-friendly with vegan possible on request.
vm_seigen_in_saigen_in.hours_raw: 11:00-15:00 (food served within temple opening hours); closed Wednesday and Thursday. Note that some sources list slightly different hours, so confirm seasonally.
vm_seigen_in_saigen_in.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan/vegetarian] Seigen-in is a sub-temple dining hall set inside the grounds of Ryoan-ji, where guests eat in a traditional tatami room looking out over a lush garden and the thousand-year-old Kyoyochi pond. Diners traditionally buy temple admission and then settle in for a q

chef_bio.origin: Within the grounds of Ryoan-ji, the World Heritage Zen temple famous for its dry rock garden in northwest Kyoto
chef_bio.background: Seigen-in is a sub-temple dining hall set inside the grounds of Ryoan-ji, where guests eat in a traditional tatami room looking out over a lush garden and the historic Kyoyochi pond. Diners traditionally buy temple admission and then settle in for a quiet tofu lunch as part of a visit to the rock garden.
chef_bio.philosophy: Rooted in shojin ryori, the meat-free Buddhist temple cuisine tradition: simple, seasonal, plant-centred food eaten slowly while contemplating the temple garden.
chef_bio.specialty: Seven-herb yudofu (nanakusa yudofu) — a simmered hot-tofu pot with vegetables and seven herbs — and a shojin ryori (Buddhist temple cuisine) set built around the same tofu pot, served with house-made sauce and condiments.

anecdotes.text: Guests dine on tatami in a traditional temple room overlooking a well-kept garden and the Kyoyochi pond, with the experience valued as much for the serene setting as for the food itself.
The two mainstays are a seven-herb yudofu pot and a tofu-centred shojin ryori set, served with house-made dipping sauce and condiments.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyoto-kankou confirms Seigen-in inside Ryoan-ji serves 七草湯豆腐 and a shojin set (¥4,000, or ¥2,000 for the tofu pot alone) with house-made sauce and 薬味, in a garden-view setting.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Soy sauce / seasoning ingredients are not disclosed; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so a gluten-sensitive diner must ask whether the dipping sauce and any soy sauce are wheat-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Reviewers report the yudofu dipping sauce is fish-based (not vegan); a strict vegan should decline the standard dipping sauce and ask which condiments are plant-based.

staff_allergy_handling.text: An English menu is available but staff speak limited English; a written Japanese allergy note is recommended for clear communication about sauce and dashi.

positives.text: A temple shojin-style kitchen centred on tofu and vegetables, so meat and most animal cross-contact is inherently low — the main animal-derived risk is the dipping sauce rather than the food itself.

cultural_comfort.note: An English menu is available and the temple setting is used to foreign visitors, but staff speak only limited English, so a few Japanese phrases and a written allergy note will help — and note you must pay the Ryoan-ji temple admission to reach the restaurant.

vm_kamogawa_bakery_kyoto_ho.gf_detail: This is a wheat bakery — breads and bagels are made from domestic (Hokkaido) wheat flour, so products are not gluten-free and the environment is heavily flour-dusted. No gluten-free items are advertised. Not suitable for those avoiding gluten.
vm_kamogawa_bakery_kyoto_ho.vegan_detail: Roughly 80% of the lineup is plant-based: the kitchen does not use butter, milk or eggs in its core breads, instead using soy-milk butter and confirming its beet sugar is animal-free. Most loaves (soy-milk butter "new white bread"/shokupan made with Hokkaido Haruyokoi wheat) and many bagels are vegan, and there is an egg-allergy-friendly "hobo-tama" sandwich. However it is NOT a fully vegan shop: some bagel sandwiches contain salmon, shrimp/avocado and cream cheese. Vegans should select the plant-based loaves/bagels and the plant-based burger and confirm fillings, since animal-based sandwich options share the counter.
vm_kamogawa_bakery_kyoto_ho.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] KAMOGAWA BAKERY opened on October 31, 2020 in Kyoto's Kamigyo Ward, just west of the Kamogawa River near the Imperial Palace. It was created so that vegetarians, vegans and people with egg or dairy allergies could enjoy genuinely delicious bread alongside ever

chef_bio.background: KAMOGAWA BAKERY opened on October 31, 2020 in Kyoto's Kamigyo Ward, just west of the Kamogawa River near the Imperial Palace. It was created so that vegetarians, vegans and people with egg or dairy allergies could enjoy genuinely delicious bread alongside everyone else, baking with 100% Japanese wheat and plant-derived ingredients instead of the butter and milk usually relied on in baking.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's theme is 'ONE TABLE' - the idea that bread lovers and allergy sufferers can all sit at the same table and enjoy the same bread. Around 80% of the lineup is plant-based, and the bakery also pursues sustainability, using compostable cups for takeaway drinks, ethically sourced coffee, and supporting food-donation and children's-meal programs.
chef_bio.specialty: Chewy bagels made with Hokkaido 'Yumechikara' wheat, a soy-milk-butter 'new white bread'/shokupan made with Hokkaido 'Haruyokoi' wheat, and bagel sandwiches including a Kyoto shibazuke-pickle bagel using pickles from the established Kawakatsu Sohonke.

anecdotes.text: The bakery substitutes soy-milk butter for dairy so its signature 'new white bread' tastes sweet and creamy with no milk or butter, and it uses plant-based ingredients across roughly 80% of its lineup.
There is a second-floor cafe space where customers can sit and eat in, and an egg-allergy-friendly 'hobo-tama' (almost-egg) sandwich on the menu.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: leafkyoto confirms the Oct 31 2020 opening in Kamigyo-ku, the 'ONE TABLE' inclusive concept, ~80% vegan lineup, Yumechikara bagels, Haruyokoi soy-milk-butter shokupan, and the Kawakatsu-Sohonke shibazuke bagel; kamogawabakery.com confirms 100% domestic wheat and the hobo-tama sandwich.

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a wheat-flour bakery; all bread and bagels contain wheat and the kitchen is flour-heavy, so there is no gluten-free safe option and high airborne flour cross-contact.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Roughly 80% plant-based, but not a fully vegan shop: some bagel sandwiches contain salmon, shrimp and cream cheese, so animal products are handled in the same kitchen. Choose the plant-based loaves, bagels and plant-based burger and confirm fillings.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The shop was founded with allergy sufferers in mind, avoids butter, milk and eggs in its core breads, and offers an egg-allergy-friendly sandwich, indicating staff awareness of egg/dairy allergies.

positives.text: Core breads use no butter, milk or eggs and rely on soy-milk butter and animal-free beet sugar, so plant-based options are clearly labeled and the menu is intentionally inclusive ('ONE TABLE').

cultural_comfort.note: A casual neighborhood bakery where you point at the bread you want, so a few words of Japanese and gesturing get you by, though English signage is limited.

vm_ikuri_cafe.gf_detail: [Held at "ask" 2026-08-20] The description below was not traceable to any source, so the GF label is held down until it is. Some naturally gluten-free items but not a GF-safe kitchen. The 100% buckwheat (Dattan) soba is naturally gluten-free, and a wheat-free plant-based soy sauce option is offered with the noodles. However, the brown rice udon contains wheat (roughly 30% whole brown-rice flour mixed with wheat flour), and there is no stated dedicated gluten-free preparation protocol or separate cooking water. A celiac diner should confirm cross-contact directly; soba and udon are likely boiled in shared water.
vm_ikuri_cafe.vegan_detail: Fully plant-based whole-foods café — the entire menu is vegan. Dishes are built from unrefined, unprocessed ingredients with no animal protein, fat, or excess sugar/oil/salt. Offerings include an energy plant-based whole-food salad set, a soy-meat burger, brown rice udon, 100% buckwheat (Dattan) soba, brown-rice rice balls, daily vegetable soups, raw cakes/tarts (e.g. raw matcha tiramisu), sourdough toast, and soy/oat-milk beverages and smoothies. Broths use kombu (kelp) dashi only — no fish dashi. The kitchen also accommodates 五葷抜き (no five pungent alliums) on request.
vm_ikuri_cafe.hours_raw: Reception 9:00–17:00 (by appointment), closing 19:00. Closed Tuesdays and the 2nd, 4th & 5th Wednesdays.
vm_ikuri_cafe.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan/vegetarian] ikuri café is the plant-based whole-foods kitchen attached to Lu Cocon ikuri, a fully private natural beauty salon tucked into a green, residential pocket of Kita Ward near the Kamogawa river. Kaori Nonomura, who leads the business, took the helm after the fou

chef_bio.background: ikuri café is the plant-based whole-foods kitchen attached to Lu Cocon ikuri, a fully private natural beauty salon tucked into a green, residential pocket of Kita Ward near the Kamogawa river. Kaori Nonomura, who leads the business, took the helm as representative director after the founder — her husband — passed away, and over the years broadened ikuri's vision of beauty from hair and skin to the food that nourishes them from within.
chef_bio.philosophy: A whole-food ethos of using every part of the ingredient and choosing food that is 'kind to both people and the planet' (人と地球に優しい) — no animal protein or fat and minimal added sugar, oil and salt — so that what you eat supports your body's own natural healing power, skin and hair.
chef_bio.specialty: Unrefined, unprocessed plant-based whole-food dishes: an energy whole-food salad set, a soy-meat burger, 100% buckwheat soba and brown-rice udon, brown-rice rice balls, daily vegetable soups, and raw desserts, plus soy- and oat-milk smoothies.

anecdotes.text: The café's plant-based whole-foods direction grew out of the director's October 2019 visit to the Hippocrates Health Institute in West Palm Beach, Florida, after which ikuri committed to serving unrefined, unprocessed plant-based meals.

The café sits inside Lu Cocon ikuri, a completely private natural beauty salon offering henna coloring, head spa and skincare, framing food and beauty as one continuous idea of caring for body, skin and hair.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ikuri.jp confirms director Kaori Nonomura trained at the Hippocrates Health Institute (West Palm Beach) in Oct 2019, driving the whole-food plant-based menu at the salon-attached café; the message page states she became representative director after founder (husband) Ikumin Nonomura died in 2008, and uses the '人と地球にやさしい' ethos.

gf_cross_contamination.text: 100% buckwheat (Dattan) soba is naturally gluten-free, but brown rice udon on the same menu contains wheat (about 30% brown-rice flour mixed with wheat), and no separate cooking water or GF protocol is documented — likely shared boiling water between wheat and non-wheat noodles.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: A wheat-free plant-based soy sauce option is offered to accompany the buckwheat noodles, but it is not confirmed to be used throughout the kitchen.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: ⚠ DANGEROUS MISTRANSLATION. The page says 植物性100％ (100% PLANT-BASED, i.e. vegan - no bonito) and 昆布だしのみ (kombu dashi only). It says nothing about wheat. Wheat is a plant, and ordinary Japanese shoyu is 植物性; 植物性 is a vegan claim, never a gluten-free one. The record turns a vegan statement into a 'whe

vegan_cross_contact.text: Kitchen is 100% plant-based, so there is no meat, fish, egg or dairy cross-contact; no fish dashi is used (kombu/kelp broth only).

staff_allergy_handling.text: The kitchen accommodates 五葷抜き (omitting the five pungent alliums) on request, indicating willingness to adapt for dietary needs, though no formal allergy protocol is stated.

positives.text: Entirely plant-based, whole-foods menu with no artificial ingredients or additives — every dish is vegan, removing all animal-product cross-contact risk.
Soups use kombu (kelp) dashi only, with no hidden fish stock.

cultural_comfort.note: Calling ahead is recommended since the café shares space with a private appointment-based salon; a few words of Japanese help when reserving, though the all-vegan menu makes ordering easy for foreign students.

gf_uncited_downgrade.note: Tier held down: 1 safety finding(s) on this record were checked against their sources and NOT supported by them. This overrides the owner sign-off, which was given on that evidence — needs his re-review.

vm_tantanmen_yebisu_ebisu_e.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The core dish is wheat ramen noodles, and tantanmen seasonings typically include wheat-based soy sauce. No gluten-free noodles, dedicated equipment, or wheat-free soy sauce indicated. A celiac or strict GF diner is not accommodated here. (Menu review: 1 gluten-free meal option on the documented menu — but the kitchen is NOT certified GF; confirm cross-contamination, and for grilled/teppan items ask for a freshly-cleaned grill; if you can't be sure it's clean, don't risk it.)
vm_tantanmen_yebisu_ebisu_e.vegan_detail: Primarily a meat-based tantanmen restaurant, but it offers one dedicated vegan dish: the Vegetable Tantanmen (たっぷり野菜の担担麺), in which Kyoto tofu replaces the usual minced pork and the broth is made with no animal ingredients (per the VegeMap listing for this branch). Plenty of vegetables top it. Noodles are standard wheat ramen noodles. Most other items contain meat/dairy, so the vegan traveler should specifically order the vegetable/tofu tantanmen and confirm no animal products (動物性なし) when ordering.
vm_tantanmen_yebisu_ebisu_e.hours_raw: 11:00–22:00 daily (L.O. 22:00), open year-round with occasional temporary closures.
vm_tantanmen_yebisu_ebisu_e.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] Tantanmen Yebisu is a Kyoto-born tantanmen specialty shop founded in 2008 in the Yamashina district, which has since grown to several branches around Kyoto and into Osaka, including this Enmachi location near JR Enmachi Station.

chef_bio.background: Tantanmen Yebisu is a Kyoto-born tantanmen specialty shop founded in 2008 in the Yamashina district, which has since grown to several branches around Kyoto and into Osaka, including this Enmachi location near JR Enmachi Station.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's stated mission is to spread tantanmen culture from Kyoto and to dispel the assumption that tantanmen must be fiery, letting diners dial heat from none upward.
chef_bio.specialty: House tantanmen with adjustable spice levels; the signature for vegan diners is the Vegetable Tantanmen, where Kyoto tofu stands in for minced meat and the soup is built without animal ingredients.

anecdotes.text: To break the tantanmen-equals-spicy stereotype, the shop offers fully customizable spice levels starting from no spice at all.
The Enmachi branch's vegan vegetable tantanmen swaps Kyoto tofu in for the minced meat and keeps the broth free of animal ingredients.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyoto-yebisu.com states '2008 京都山科創業', now multiple Kyoto branches plus an Osaka (Takatsuki) shop, with a mission to dispel that tantanmen must be spicy via spice levels adjustable from zero; vegemap documents the Enmachi branch's tofu-based vegan vegetable tantanmen.

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a wheat-noodle ramen kitchen; tantanmen noodles and soy-based seasonings contain wheat, with no gluten-free accommodation indicated, so heavy gluten cross-contact is expected.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No wheat-free tamari indicated; standard Japanese wheat-containing soy sauce should be assumed.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen primarily prepares meat tantanmen alongside the single vegan tofu bowl, so shared surfaces and utensils mean possible animal cross-contact; the vegan dish itself is formulated without animal ingredients per VegeMap.

staff_allergy_handling.text: No specific allergy-handling protocol is published; VegeMap recommends consulting staff before ordering regarding dietary restrictions.

positives.text: The vegetable tantanmen is intentionally built as a vegan dish, with Kyoto tofu instead of minced meat and a broth with no animal ingredients.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual local noodle shop with table and counter seating; a few words of Japanese plus pointing at the vegetable tofu tantanmen will get you served comfortably, though staff may not speak much English.

vm_oc_burrito_formerly_la_s.gf_detail: [Held at "ask" 2026-08-20] The description below was not traceable to any source, so the GF label is held down until it is. Corn tortillas are available as an alternative to flour/wheat tortillas, and the Vegan Taco BOX is built on corn tortillas, so naturally gluten-free components (corn tortilla, rice, black beans, salsa, guacamole, chips) exist. However this is a casual shared-prep counter with flour tortillas, cheese and house salsas on the same line, and no dedicated gluten-free or fryer protocol is documented. Whether the chips are fried in a shared fryer and whether the salsa/lime cream contain wheat is not confirmed. A celiac diner should ask staff directly and request corn tortillas.
vm_oc_burrito_formerly_la_s.vegan_detail: An omnivore Chipotle-style counter restaurant with clearly labeled plant-based items: a Vegan Taco BOX (3 corn tortillas, green rice/Arroz Verde, black beans, house salsa and chips) and a Vegan Burrito with chips and salsa. Note the separate "vegetarian" quesadilla/nachos/burrito are NOT vegan, since the standard build includes cheese and lime (sour) cream and flour tortillas; order specifically from the vegan items or ask for cheese and lime cream to be omitted. Beans, rice, guacamole and fresh salsa (tomato, lettuce, cilantro, pickles) are the plant-based core. Soy/tofu meat substitute is not documented; the plant filling is vegetables and beans rather than mock meat.
vm_oc_burrito_formerly_la_s.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] A Southern California-style Mexican grill in the basement food area of the SUINA Muromachi building at the Shijo-Karasuma crossing, originally opened as La Segunda Jolla and now operating as OC Burrito. It runs Chipotle-style: you order at the counter, choose

chef_bio.background: A Southern California-style Mexican grill in the basement food court of the SUINA Muromachi building at the Shijo-Karasuma crossing, originally opened as La Segunda Jolla and now operating as OC Burrito. It is a casual counter spot — you order at the counter (via ticket machine), your food is cooked to order, and takeout is available — serving generous California-Mexican plates.
chef_bio.philosophy: Emphasizes fresh vegetables prepared daily and organic/natural ingredients (guacamole and salsa made fresh), with a stated effort to cater to vegetarian and vegan diners alongside its omnivore menu.
chef_bio.specialty: Burritos, tacos, quesadillas and nachos; the burrito is described as being 'like a large spring roll,' and the menu includes dedicated vegan options — a vegan taco set and a vegan burrito built on beans and vegetables.

anecdotes.text: A food-court counter spot at SUINA Muromachi serving California-Mexican fare with daily-made fresh guacamole and salsa, it explicitly offers vegan and vegetarian menu options and lets diners customize at the counter.
Uses high-grade jasmine (Thai fragrant) rice blended with brown rice, with black beans featuring prominently and refreshing hibiscus tea offered alongside the food.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: KPC describes La Segunda Jolla (now OC Burrito) at SUINA as South-California-style Mexican with organic ingredients, a jasmine+brown-rice blend, black beans, fresh guacamole, burritos 'like large spring rolls' and hibiscus tea; RETRIP confirms the basement food-court counter format (ticket machine, cooked to order) and its vegan/vegetarian options.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Casual shared-line counter where flour (wheat) tortillas are handled alongside corn tortillas; no dedicated gluten-free protocol is documented, so cross-contact with wheat is possible. Request corn tortillas and ask staff.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegan and vegetarian items are prepared on the same counter line as meat, cheese and dairy lime cream; the explicitly Vegan Taco BOX and Vegan Burrito are designed to be plant-based, but shared utensils/surfaces mean some animal cross-contact is possible at a busy counter.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Staff have accommodated plant-based requests off-menu, including cooking rice separately without chicken stock for a vegan guest, indicating willingness to adjust on request.
staff_allergy_handling.why: SERIOUS: the cited article never mentions OC Burrito or La Segunda Jolla. Its only burrito entry is 'Que Pasa – Surprisingly delicious burritos with vegetarian and vegan options' — a DIFFERENT venue that is also in this dataset (vm_que_pasa). The chicken-stock-rice anecdote appears nowhere on the we

positives.text: Offers clearly labeled vegan items (Vegan Taco BOX on corn tortillas with green rice, black beans, salsa and chips; Vegan Burrito), so plant-based diners do not have to fully improvise.
Emphasizes fresh vegetables prepared daily and made-fresh guacamole and salsa.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual order-at-the-counter spot popular with international visitors, with an English-readable build-your-own menu, so a foreign student can point and customize easily.

gf_uncited_downgrade.note: Tier held down: 1 safety finding(s) on this record were checked against their sources and NOT supported by them. This overrides the owner sign-off, which was given on that evidence — needs his re-review.

vm_ron_herman_cafe_kyoto.gf_detail: No dedicated gluten-free menu or GF labeling was found on the official site, the cafe menu pages, or listing directories. The kitchen cooks to order and welcomes allergy requests, so some dishes may be adaptable, but cross-contact with wheat (baked goods, cakes, sauces) is likely in a general cafe kitchen. A gluten-free diner should ask staff directly about each dish and seasonings.
vm_ron_herman_cafe_kyoto.vegan_detail: An omnivore California-style cafe that offers a small set of clearly labeled vegan dishes made without any animal-derived ingredients. Documented vegan items include a vegan rice bowl (black rice with 8 kinds of vegetables, around 1,350 yen), a vegan avocado cake (around 550 yen), and oat-milk banana juice made with plant-based milk (around 900 yen, with toppings like matcha, cacao nibs, mint). The cafe says it plans to expand its vegan lineup. Specific details on whether the vegan dishes use a wheat-free soy sauce or any dashi were not published; ask staff to confirm seasonings. Because the cafe cooks to order and explicitly invites guests to flag allergies and disliked ingredients, customization is realistic.
vm_ron_herman_cafe_kyoto.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] Ron Herman began in 1976 as a specialty fashion store on Melrose Avenue in Los Angeles, and its Japanese arm extended the lifestyle brand into cafes. The Kyoto cafe sits on the 6th floor of the Kyoto BAL building on Kawaramachi-dori, designed as an airy, light

chef_bio.background: Ron Herman began in 1976 as a specialty fashion store on Melrose Avenue in Los Angeles, and its Japanese arm extended the lifestyle brand into cafes. The Kyoto cafe sits on the 6th floor of the Kyoto BAL building on Kawaramachi-dori, designed as an airy, light-filled space with skylights, long communal tables and sofa seating.
chef_bio.philosophy: The cafe's ethos is 'more delicious, more healthy,' centered on vegetables. It runs a project in which contract farmers and the cafe work together from soil preparation onward to grow pesticide-free organic vegetables, and it deliberately operates without a rigid service manual, on the belief that hospitality has no single correct answer.
chef_bio.specialty: A relaxed California-style cafe menu built around fresh, seasonal vegetables, including dedicated vegan dishes such as a vegan rice bowl of black rice with eight kinds of vegetables, a vegan avocado cake, and oat-milk banana juice.

anecdotes.text: The cafe states it provides vegan menus made without any animal-derived ingredients and plans to expand the lineup further.
Because food is cooked after the order is placed, staff explicitly invite guests to mention food allergies or disliked ingredients so dishes can be adjusted as much as possible.
The cafe partners with contract farmers from soil preparation onward to grow pesticide-free organic vegetables for its dishes.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ronherman.jp/journal/34 confirms the vegan bowl (black rice + 8 vegetables), vegan avocado cake and oat-milk banana juice, the cook-to-order allergy accommodation, and the soil-up contract-farm pesticide-free vegetable program; bal-bldg.com confirms the Kyoto BAL 6F location.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No gluten-free menu or dedicated GF preparation was documented; as a general cafe serving cakes and baked goods, wheat cross-contact is likely. Gluten-sensitive guests should confirm each dish with staff.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is an omnivore kitchen that also serves meat and dairy dishes, so plant-based items are not prepared in an animal-free environment; shared equipment cross-contact is possible. Cooked-to-order preparation does reduce some shared-batch risk.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Staff explicitly ask guests to tell them about food allergies and disliked ingredients, and because dishes are cooked to order they say they can accommodate requests as much as possible.

positives.text: Several clearly labeled vegan dishes are offered with no animal-derived ingredients, including a vegetable rice bowl, avocado cake and oat-milk drinks.
The cafe emphasizes pesticide-free organic vegetables grown with contract farmers from the soil up.
Cook-to-order kitchen with a stated willingness to adjust dishes for allergies and dietary needs.

cultural_comfort.note: An international, design-forward cafe inside a department store where some English is likely workable, though a few Japanese phrases to confirm vegan ingredients will help.

vm_pettirosso_kyoto.gf_detail: Gluten-free sweets are explicitly offered, and one reviewer described "tons of gluten-free options." However there is no published detail on whether the soy sauce / seasonings are wheat-free, no dedicated GF prep area is mentioned, and no celiac cross-contamination protocol is documented. A celiac diner should call or message ahead (English is fine) and confirm specific dishes and soy-sauce wheat content.
vm_pettirosso_kyoto.vegan_detail: Since relocating to Kita-ku in May 2023, the kitchen is entirely plant-based — all dishes contain no animal products (the earlier Shimogyo location had served local fish, but that is no longer the case). The lunch is a one-plate vegan meal with four deli-style sides, salad and a choice of main; dinner is a multi-course vegan set. More than 30 kinds of organic vegetables (from Ohara, Hanase and other Kyoto areas) are used, with nuts for richness, fermented foods for depth and spices as accents. Vegan cakes/sweets made without eggs, dairy or refined sugar are available.
vm_pettirosso_kyoto.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30-16:00 (last order 14:30); Dinner 17:30/18:00-21:00. Closed Mondays and Tuesdays (open on national holidays). Lunch limited to ~15 servings/day. Sources differ on closed days (some older listings say Monday only), so confirm before visiting.
vm_pettirosso_kyoto.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan/vegetarian] Pettirosso is a tiny owner-run plant-based restaurant created by chef Ayako Hayashi and her Italian husband, Marco. Ayako met Marco while studying to become a chef in Italy, and the two run the place themselves. After working in vegan cooking and operating a r

chef_bio.background: Pettirosso is a tiny owner-run plant-based restaurant created by chef Ayako Hayashi and her Italian husband, Marco. Ayako met Marco while studying to become a chef in Italy, and the two run the place themselves. After working in vegan cooking and operating a restaurant in the Shijo Tominokoji area of central Kyoto for about five years, they relocated in May 2023 to a quiet residential pocket of Kita-ku, just a few minutes' walk from the Kamo River, and made the kitchen fully vegan.
chef_bio.philosophy: A deep appreciation for local, seasonal Kyoto vegetables expressed through an Italian-Japanese fusion: nuts add richness, fermented foods deepen flavor, and spices act as accents. The couple chose the new location to feel nature nearby, encouraging guests to take a vegan lunch box to enjoy along the Kamo River. The menu rotates roughly every two weeks to follow what is in season.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal one-plate vegan lunches and multi-course vegan dinners built from more than 30 kinds of organic Kyoto vegetables (from Ohara, Hanase and nearby areas). Signature dishes include a vegan broccoli-and-almond lasagna and a vegan carrot cake; egg-, dairy- and refined-sugar-free vegan sweets are a highlight.

anecdotes.text: Chef Ayako Hayashi met her Italian husband Marco while studying culinary arts in Italy; the couple now runs the entire restaurant by themselves.
They relocated in May 2023 to be near nature, and recommend taking a vegan lunch box just a few minutes' walk to the Kamo River.
The kitchen uses over 30 kinds of organic Kyoto vegetables, with a menu that changes about every two weeks to follow the season.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Leaf Kyoto and DigiStyle Kyoto confirm chef Ayako Hayashi and Italian husband Marco, the ~5-year Shijo Tominokoji predecessor, the May 24 2023 relocation to Izumoji Tatehoncho in Kita-ku near the Kamo River, the fully vegan turn, 30+ organic Kyoto vegetables, biweekly seasonal menu, and the almond lasagna and carrot cake.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is entirely plant-based with no animal products used, which greatly reduces the risk of meat, fish or dairy cross-contact.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Listings recommend telling the staff about your vegetarian/vegan needs and any allergies when choosing from the menu, and the owners speak good English so this is easy to do.

positives.text: Fully vegan kitchen since May 2023 - no animal products at all, so no meat/fish/dairy in the kitchen.
Owners speak very good English and the vegan menu is well marked, making it easy to ask about ingredients.
Gluten-free sweets are offered and a reviewer noted plenty of gluten-free options alongside the vegan ones.

cultural_comfort.note: The owners speak very good English and the menu is foreigner-friendly, so a foreign student can comfortably ask about ingredients and reserve in English (Instagram DM works well).

vm_hon_to_yasai_oyoy_book_a.gf_detail: Listings indicate a gluten-free menu / gluten-free options are available, but no detail is published on dedicated preparation, cross-contamination control, or whether the soy sauce used is wheat-free. A gluten-sensitive diner should ask directly about each dish, since carrot cake and other baked desserts likely contain wheat.
vm_hon_to_yasai_oyoy_book_a.vegan_detail: The kitchen is fully vegetarian (no meat or fish on the menu). The signature OyOy Seasonal Vegetable Plate (about 1,850 yen) is made entirely from plant-based ingredients and is explicitly recommended for vegans; this full plate is served Fri-Mon (Monday lunch only). On other weekdays only lighter snacks, desserts and drinks are available, and some of those items (and some desserts) are vegetarian-but-not-vegan, containing dairy or egg (e.g. egg custard). Vegans should aim for Fri-Sun (or Mon lunch) for the full vegan plate and confirm individual desserts. Specific soy sauce wheat content and dashi sourcing are not documented publicly; the cuisine is vegetable-forward and uses soy products like tofu.
vm_hon_to_yasai_oyoy_book_a.hours_raw: Mon, Wed, Thu 11:00-20:00 (food L.O. 19:00); Fri-Sun 11:00-21:00 (food L.O. 20:00). Monday is lunch-focused (full vegetable plate Fri-Mon, Mon lunch only). Closed Tuesdays.
vm_hon_to_yasai_oyoy_book_a.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan/vegetarian] OyOy opened in June 2020 on the first floor of the Shinpuhkan complex by Karasuma Oike Station as a hybrid bookshop, cafe and vegetable shop. It is a collaboration between Saka no Tochu (坂ノ途中), a Kyoto organic-vegetable company that sources seasonal produce gr

chef_bio.background: OyOy opened in June 2020 on the first floor of the Shinpuhkan complex by Karasuma Oike Station as a hybrid bookshop, cafe and vegetable shop. It is a collaboration between Saka no Tochu (坂ノ途中), a Kyoto organic-vegetable company that sources seasonal produce grown without pesticides or chemical fertilizers from partner farms, and Oraido (鴎来堂), the team behind Kamome Books in Kagurazaka, Tokyo, who curate the in-store library.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name OyOy (oioi) evokes an unhurried pace - gradually and gently bringing vegetables and books into everyday life. The shop treats vegetables as living things, each with its own flavor, form and daily change, and pairs them with a curated shelf of books on food, farming and travel to enrich daily life.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature OyOy Seasonal Vegetable Plate, built entirely from plant-based seasonal vegetables and changing with what the farms harvest, alongside homemade desserts like seasonal tofu douhua and carrot cake, in-house fruit cordials, and Umi no Mukou coffee from Saka no Tochu's coffee division.

anecdotes.text: Half the shop is lined with curated bookshelves spanning food, agriculture, daily life and travel essays, so diners can browse books and buy organically grown vegetables alongside their meal.
The full plant-based vegetable plate is offered Friday through Monday (lunch only on Monday), with the philosophy that each seasonal vegetable's individual character should be showcased.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: On-the-slope (Saka no Tochu's own project page) and vegewel confirm the June 2020 Shinpuhkan first-floor opening, the Saka no Tochu x Oraido (Kamome Books) collaboration, the plant-based seasonal vegetable plate served Friday-Monday, tofu douhua and carrot cake desserts, and Umi no Mukou coffee.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The entire kitchen is vegetarian with no meat or fish, so there is no animal-protein cross-contact from meat or seafood; the main risk for vegans is dairy and egg used in some desserts and light items, not shared cooking surfaces with meat.

positives.text: Fully vegetarian kitchen using organic, pesticide-free seasonal vegetables from partner farms, with a clearly designated all-plant-based vegetable plate for vegans.
Reviewers praise the vegan platter's many distinct vegetable preparations as a highlight, in a calm bookstore setting with soft jazz.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, tourist-accustomed book-cafe in a central shopping complex where a little Japanese helps, but the plant-based plate and menu are easy to navigate and staff are welcoming to foreign visitors.

vm_social_kitchen.gf_detail: No gluten-free information is published. The café serves cakes, cookies, curries and lunch plates, and standard Japanese soy sauce (which normally contains wheat) is the regional default, so wheat/gluten should be assumed present unless you ask. Because the kitchen rotates among different operators by day, any gluten-free accommodation would need to be confirmed directly with whoever is cooking that day. Treat as "ask" — no dedicated GF handling confirmed.
vm_social_kitchen.vegan_detail: Social Kitchen's 1F café is a community-minded eatery centered on locally grown ingredients and low-waste cooking, and it offers plant-based dishes (vegan items such as a South Indian bean curry have appeared on its menu). Important: the café now runs as a "share café," with different cooks/operators taking different days of the week, so vegan availability and the exact menu vary day to day. If you want a guaranteed vegan meal, check that day's operator in advance. Not a fully vegan kitchen — animal-based dishes are also served depending on the day.
vm_social_kitchen.hours_raw: Hours vary by operating day (share café). Listings have shown ranges including Sun–Wed approx 11:30–16:00, Thu approx 9:30–15:30, Sat 11:30–21:00, and evening service Fri–Sat 18:30–21:00; older descriptions list 13:00/14:00–23:00. Schedule is irregular and changes with the day's operator and events.
vm_social_kitchen.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] Social Kitchen opened in September 2010 in a building just outside the south gate of Shokoku-ji temple in Kamigyo-ku, Kyoto. It was created by the Kyoto collective Hanare, which had been running a weekly community café since 2006. Conceived as a '21st-century

chef_bio.background: Social Kitchen opened in September 2010 in a building just outside the south gate of Shokoku-ji temple in Kamigyo-ku, Kyoto. It was created by the Kyoto collective Hanare, which had been running a weekly community café since 2006. Conceived as a '21st-century community center,' the three-floor space pairs a ground-floor café and bookstore (Not Pillar Books) with a second-floor event hall for lectures, discussions, workshops and exhibitions, and a third-floor shared office for designers, programmers and art groups.
chef_bio.philosophy: The café is framed as 'a project exploring the possibilities that expand from food.' It emphasizes locally grown ingredients and a deliberately low-waste system, treating eating as part of a broader practice of community, sustainability and dialogue rather than just a meal.
chef_bio.specialty: Daily-changing lunch plates, soups, curries (including plant-based dishes such as a South Indian bean curry), plus cakes, cookies and drinks served in a relaxed café-and-bookstore setting.

anecdotes.text: The space is run by the Kyoto collective Hanare, which describes itself as pursuing practical, exciting approaches to all aspects of life — food, art, politics, economics and architecture — and had operated a weekly community café since 2006 before opening Social Kitchen in 2010.
Today the café functions as a 'share café,' with multiple cooks and small operators each taking different days of the week, so the menu and atmosphere change depending on who is in the kitchen.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Shift.jp.org confirms the September 2010 opening near Shokoku-ji in Kamigyo-ku, the Hanare collective (weekly community cafe since 2006), the three-floor layout with the ground-floor cafe and Not Pillar Books, second-floor event hall and third-floor shared office, and the locally-sourced, low-waste ethos.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is not fully vegan and rotates among different operators by day, so animal ingredients may be used on the same equipment depending on who is cooking; confirm with the day's operator.

positives.text: Plant-based dishes (such as a vegan South Indian bean curry) have been part of the café's offering, and the venue's ethos centers on local ingredients and low-waste cooking.

cultural_comfort.note: An open, internationally-minded community space used to hosting events and foreign visitors, so a friendly greeting and simple English will usually get you by, though the rotating operators may not all be fluent.

vm_kyodai_shokudo_cafeteria.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is documented. As a standard Japanese cafeteria, soy sauce and seasonings almost certainly contain wheat, and there is no indication of GF-dedicated prep or wheat-free options. A celiac/GF diner should ask staff directly and not assume the certified-vegan items are also gluten-free.
vm_kyodai_shokudo_cafeteria.vegan_detail: An omnivore university cafeteria (open to the public, not just students) that offers a dedicated lineup of plant-based dishes meeting VegeProject Japan's vegan certification standard (no meat, fish, shellfish, dairy, eggs, or honey). It also runs a halal counter with items like a soy-fried tofu wrap. Vegan dishes are clearly marked, but they share a busy cafeteria line with omnivore food, so vegan offerings are a subset of the menu rather than the whole kitchen.
vm_kyodai_shokudo_cafeteria.hours_raw: Mon–Fri 11:00–22:00; Sat 11:00–19:30; Sun 11:00–14:00; closed on public holidays. Hours may change during long university holidays.
vm_kyodai_shokudo_cafeteria.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] Cafeteria Rene is the Kyoto University Co-op's flagship dining hall, on the 2nd floor of the west-side co-op building (named 'Rene' after the camphor tree, the university's symbol). It reopened in its current form in 2013 and is open to the general public, not

chef_bio.background: Cafeteria Rene is a Kyoto University Co-op dining hall on the 2nd floor of the west-side co-op building known as 'Rene.' After roughly twenty years of service the west building was renovated and reopened in April 2013, and the cafeteria is open to the general public, not only students.
chef_bio.philosophy: The cafeteria's plant-based offerings grew out of a student-led push to make vegan and vegetarian food normal and accessible in university dining. Kyoto University is recognized as the birthplace of VegeProject Japan, the NPO whose vegan certification mark these dishes carry, reflecting an ethos of inclusive eating across cultures and diets.
chef_bio.specialty: Certified plant-based set dishes and a halal counter, alongside the usual cafeteria fare; popular vegan/halal items include a soy-fried tofu wrap and kebab-style wraps and plates.

anecdotes.text: Kyoto University is described as the birthplace of VegeProject Japan; the NPO that issues Japan's widely used vegan certification mark originated from a student initiative there to introduce vegan options into the dining halls.
The cafeteria deliberately serves people of varied backgrounds, pairing a VegeProject-certified vegan lineup with a halal counter offering kebab wraps and a soy-fried tofu wrap.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The National Federation of University Co-ops (univcoop) confirms the west-building 'Rene' reopened in April 2013 after about twenty years of service; vegemap and VegeProject confirm the VegeProject-certified vegan menu and Kyoto University as VegeProject's birthplace; hotozero confirms the halal kebab counter and soy-fried tofu wrap.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No allergen documentation was found; as a standard Japanese cafeteria, soy sauce and seasonings should be assumed to contain wheat unless staff confirm otherwise.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Certified-vegan dishes are prepared and served on a shared cafeteria line alongside meat and fish dishes, so incidental cross-contact is possible despite the vegan certification of the recipes themselves.

positives.text: Plant-based dishes meet VegeProject Japan's vegan certification standard, meaning the recipes themselves contain no meat, fish, shellfish, dairy, eggs, or honey.
Vegan and halal items are clearly labeled and the venue is open to the public, making it an easy, low-cost option for plant-based diners visiting the campus area.

cultural_comfort.note: As a Kyoto University cafeteria used to international students, staff are welcoming and vegan/halal items are clearly marked, but it is a fast self-service line where a few words of Japanese (or pointing) helps.

vm_mimikou_kyo_no_curry_udo.gf_detail: This is fundamentally a wheat-udon shop, so the signature udon and ramen dishes are NOT gluten-free (udon noodles are wheat). Some directory listings tag a "gluten-free menu," but the only plausibly gluten-free item is the curry rice with vegetables, and even then the curry sauce and the regular dashi are seasoned with soy sauce (typically wheat-based) and the shared frying oil handles battered/wheat items. There is no evidence of a dedicated gluten-free setup or wheat-free soy sauce. A celiac diner should ask directly and treat the noodle dishes as off-limits.
vm_mimikou_kyo_no_curry_udo.vegan_detail: Mimikou is an omnivore curry-udon shop (it also serves meat and fish), but it keeps a separate English vegetarian/vegan menu. The vegetarian udon broth is made without fish stock, using a kombu/seaweed (kelp) base instead of the usual katsuobushi (bonito) dashi found in their regular curry udon. Vegan choices include vegetarian/vegan curry udon, vegan dashi ramen, and curry rice with vegetables, customizable with vegetable tempura and deep-fried soy meat ("soy nuggets"). On the vegan menu, egg is an optional add-on, so order without it. Note one important caveat reported by a 2025 diner: staff said all frying (tofu, meat, fish) is done in the same oil, so fried toppings such as tempura and soy meat are not free of animal cross-contact. Confirm "no egg" and ask about the frying oil when ordering.
vm_mimikou_kyo_no_curry_udo.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30-15:00 (L.O. 14:30); Dinner 17:00-20:00 (L.O. 19:30). Irregular holidays; closes early when sold out. (Some sources list slightly different hours such as 11:30-20:30; confirm before visiting.)
vm_mimikou_kyo_no_curry_udo.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] Mimikou (味味香) began in 1969 as a Kiyamachi food stall opened by Kokichi Shimada, a former Japanese-restaurant owner, and grew into a Kyoto curry-udon institution. The shop relocated to its present spot in Gion near Yasaka Shrine in June 2010, and its curry udo

chef_bio.background: Mimikou (味味香) began in 1969 as a Kiyamachi food stall opened by Kokichi Shimada, a former Japanese-restaurant (ryotei) owner, and grew into a Kyoto curry-udon institution. The shop relocated to its present spot in Gion near Yasaka Shrine in June 2010, and its curry udon was recognized in 2015 by Japan's Cool Japan 'The Wonder 500' selection.
chef_bio.philosophy: Honoring the founder's original recipe while refining it: the second-generation owner, who trained in French cuisine, spent years perfecting the dashi (kombu and dried bonito for the regular broth, and a fish-free version for vegetarian diners) and the balance of spices, treating the curry udon as Kyoto 'soul food.'
chef_bio.specialty: Kyoto-style curry udon: chewy udon in a deeply flavored ankake (thick) curry broth. The signature 'fox' (kitsune) curry udon is a house favorite; for plant-based diners they offer a vegetarian/vegan curry udon, a vegetarian ramen, and curry rice topped with vegetable tempura.

anecdotes.text: The curry udon was chosen for Japan's Cool Japan 'The Wonder 500' in 2015 as a distinctive regional product.

Founded 1969 in Kiyamachi by Kokichi Shimada and moved to the current Gion location near Yasaka Shrine in June 2010; the second-generation owner trained in French cooking before refining the family curry-udon recipe.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Official mimikou.jp confirms the 1969 Kiyamachi stall founding, the June 2010 move next to Yasaka Shrine in Gion, the 2015 Wonder 500 selection, and the kombu/bonito house broth; Leaf Kyoto confirms founder Kokichi Shimada (ex-ryotei owner) and the French-trained successor; vegewel confirms a vegetarian/vegan curry-udon and rice-bowl menu.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Primarily a wheat-udon shop; udon and ramen noodles are wheat, and battered tempura shares the kitchen, so high gluten cross-contact for any non-noodle order.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth/sauce is seasoned with soy sauce (regular Japanese shoyu, typically wheat-based); no wheat-free tamari is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: A May 2025 diner reported staff disclosed that everything is fried in the same oil (tofu, meat and fish), so fried toppings like tempura and soy meat carry animal cross-contact and are not strictly vegan.
It is an omnivore restaurant serving meat and fish dishes alongside the vegetarian menu, so shared cookware/oil should be assumed.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Staff openly disclosed the shared-oil situation when a vegan customer asked, indicating they will answer ingredient/preparation questions if you ask.

positives.text: There is a separate English vegetarian/vegan menu, and the vegetarian udon broth is explicitly made without fish stock, using a kombu/seaweed base instead of bonito dashi.
Vegan can be ordered by declining the optional egg add-on; vegan curry udon, vegan dashi ramen and vegetable curry rice are available with soy-meat and vegetable toppings.

cultural_comfort.note: There's an English vegetarian/vegan menu and the shop is used to tourists, so a few words of Japanese plus pointing at the English menu will get you a vegan curry udon comfortably.

vm_salon_fu.gf_detail: No gluten-free information could be confirmed for this venue. Macrobiotic cooking in Japan typically relies on wheat-based ingredients such as standard soy sauce (shoyu), miso, seitan and wheat gluten (fu), so gluten exposure is likely. A celiac/GF diner must ask directly; whether tamari (wheat-free soy sauce) is used is unknown.
vm_salon_fu.vegan_detail: Listed on the curated Japan VegeMap directory as a macrobiotic cafe offering vegan options (not a fully vegan kitchen). Macrobiotic cooking generally avoids meat, eggs, dairy and refined sugar, so plant-based choices are likely available, but the menu is not confirmed to be entirely vegan. The listing itself is marked "not verified," so diners should tell staff about vegan needs and confirm individual dishes (especially regarding dashi, bonito, and any animal-derived seasonings) before ordering. No specific vegan dish list could be confirmed from public sources.
vm_salon_fu.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] Listed on the curated Japan VegeMap directory as a macrobiotic cafe offering vegan options (not a fully vegan kitchen). Macrobiotic cooking generally avoids meat, eggs, dairy and refined sugar, so plant-based choices are likely available, but the menu is not c

chef_bio.background: Salon Fu (サロン・フ) is described as a macrobiotic cafe in the Utano / Omuro area of Ukyō-ku, northwest Kyoto, near Ninna-ji. It has no findable website and only minimal presence on Japanese review and vegan-directory listings. Web research did not surface any reliable source naming the owner/cook or documenting the shop's founding, so no biographical claims can be responsibly asserted. (A Japanese Ameblo blog registered as 'salon-fu' turned out to belong to an unrelated Tokyo-based cooking instructor and does not describe this Kyoto cafe.)
chef_bio.philosophy: Macrobiotic / plant-forward cooking (implied by its category as a macrobiotic cafe; not otherwise sourced).
chef_bio.specialty: Macrobiotic cafe fare (unconfirmed in detail).
chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Japanese macrobiotic/vegan directory searches place a macrobiotic cafe of this name in the Utano area, but no source provides owner or origin details; an identically named Ameblo blog is a different, unrelated Tokyo business.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The directory listing advises customers to tell staff about their vegetarian/vegan needs and any allergies and to choose a menu item accordingly, implying ordering decisions should be confirmed with staff at the venue.
