cultural_comfort.note: This is a small local macrobiotic cafe with little English-facing presence, so a few words of Japanese and a clearly written note about your vegan/allergy needs will help; phone ahead (075-461-5911) before visiting since hours could not be confirmed.

vm_kyodai_shokudo_hokubu_sh.gf_detail: No dedicated gluten-free program is documented. This is a high-volume cafeteria serving fried foods, noodles (udon/ramen) and breaded items alongside vegan dishes, so cross-contact with wheat is likely. Menu cards do display allergen information (wheat is one of Japan's mandatory labeled allergens), so a diner can check individual items, but GF travelers should ask staff directly. Japanese soy sauce and standard dashi-based seasonings commonly used in cafeteria cooking typically contain wheat; assume soy sauce is NOT wheat-free unless confirmed.
vm_kyodai_shokudo_hokubu_sh.vegan_detail: This is the North Cafeteria (Hokubu Shokudo) of Kyoto University's co-op, an omnivore student/staff canteen that is open to the public. It carries a certified vegan menu as part of the VegeProject initiative that began at Kyoto University in 2013. VegeMap lists it as having certified vegan options, where "vegan" is defined as containing no meat, seafood, eggs, dairy or honey. Vegan dishes are a small dedicated portion of an otherwise meat- and fish-heavy cafeteria menu, so it is a cafeteria-style pick-your-tray operation rather than a vegan restaurant. Vegan items are labeled, and menu cards display allergen information. Staff recommend telling them about your vegetarian/vegan needs and any allergies before choosing.
vm_kyodai_shokudo_hokubu_sh.hours_raw: Weekdays 11:00-21:00, Saturday 11:00-14:00, closed Sundays and public holidays (per VegeMap). Tabelog lists weekdays from 8:00; hours follow the academic calendar.
vm_kyodai_shokudo_hokubu_sh.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] The North Cafeteria is one of the Kyoto University co-op dining halls on the Yoshida campus and is open to the public, not just students and staff. It is part of the dining system that became the birthplace of Japan's vegan-menu movement: in 2013, a student-le

chef_bio.background: The North Cafeteria is one of the Kyoto University co-op dining halls on the Yoshida campus and is open to the public, not just students and staff. It is part of the dining system that became the birthplace of Japan's vegan-menu movement: in 2013, a student-led effort to put certified vegan dishes onto the university cafeteria trays grew into VegeProject, later the nonprofit VegeProject Japan.
chef_bio.philosophy: Make plant-based eating an everyday, accessible default in ordinary dining halls so that vegan, vegetarian and curious diners alike can always find a clearly labeled option.
chef_bio.specialty: Certified plant-based set meals served alongside the standard Japanese cafeteria fare, containing no meat, seafood, eggs, dairy or honey.

anecdotes.text: Kyoto University is widely cited as the birthplace of VegeProject, which began in 2013 to introduce a vegan menu to the university cafeteria and later grew into a nationwide nonprofit.
VegeProject was started by Haruko Kawano, who studied at Kyoto University and launched the cafeteria vegan-menu project in her final year of graduate school.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: VegeProject's own pages and corroborating searches confirm Kyoto University as VegeProject's birthplace, the 2013 start of the cafeteria vegan menu, and that director Haruko Kawano launched the project in her final graduate year; the specific faculty she studied in is not clearly published, so it is left unstated.

gf_cross_contamination.text: High-volume cafeteria serving fried foods and wheat noodles alongside vegan dishes; wheat cross-contact is likely and no gluten-free protocol is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No wheat-free soy sauce is confirmed; standard Japanese soy sauce and cafeteria seasonings typically contain wheat, so assume soy sauce is not gluten-free unless verified with staff.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegan dishes are prepared and served in a shared omnivore cafeteria line; the vegan menu itself is certified to contain no animal-derived ingredients, but cross-contact in a shared kitchen is possible.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Menu cards display nutritional balance and allergen information; staff recommend telling them about vegetarian/vegan needs and any allergies before choosing a dish.

positives.text: Carries a VegeProject-certified vegan menu defined as containing no meat, seafood, eggs, dairy or honey, with items clearly labeled.
Open to the public (not only students), making the certified vegan options accessible to travelers.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual university canteen with labeled vegan dishes and allergen-marked menu cards; basic Japanese or pointing helps, and as the birthplace of VegeProject it is welcoming to vegan and international diners.

vm_browny_bread_bagels.gf_detail: This is a wheat-flour bakery built around bagels, bread and focaccia made from domestic wheat with long fermentation. No gluten-free products, separate prep, or GF accommodations were found in any source. Not suitable for celiac or gluten-avoiding diners.
vm_browny_bread_bagels.vegan_detail: A wheat bakery offering 20-30 bagel varieties daily plus white bread and focaccia. Many of the plainer and savory items (made with domestic wheat, water, oil) are vegan-friendly, and soy milk is available. However, a large share of the lineup is explicitly non-vegan: cheese, cream cheese, gorgonzola-honey, tiramisu, bacon-cheese and similar varieties. There is no dedicated vegan menu or in-shop vegan labeling found, so plant-based diners should ask staff which specific bagels are egg-free and dairy-free. Confirmed as "has vegan options" rather than fully vegan.
vm_browny_bread_bagels.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] Browny Bread & Bagels is a well-loved Kyoto bagel specialist that began on Kitaoji-dori in the north of the city before relocating in 2016 to its current spot in the Shogoin neighborhood of Sakyo-ku, a short walk south of the Higashioji and Marutamachi interse

chef_bio.background: Browny Bread & Bagels is a well-loved Kyoto bagel specialist that began on Kitaoji-dori in the north of the city before relocating in 2016 to its current spot in the Shogoin neighborhood of Sakyo-ku, a short walk south of the Higashioji and Marutamachi intersection near Heian Shrine and Kyoto Zoo.
chef_bio.philosophy: The bakers emphasize carefully selected ingredients and extended, long-time fermentation to bring out the dough's fragrance, flavor and texture rather than relying on heavy fillings, with everything baked fresh on site each day.
chef_bio.specialty: Bagels above all: the shop keeps 20-30 varieties in stock at any time, made from domestic wheat with long fermentation and house-made yeast for a chewy, moist crumb and a deep wheat aroma. Signature flavors run from a popular cinnamon-apple-walnut with cream cheese to gorgonzola with honey and walnuts, kinako-mochi with red bean, sweet-potato cream cheese and bacon-cheese, alongside other savory breads. Bagels are graded by texture (firmer T-60 vs. softer T-70).

anecdotes.text: The shop consistently keeps 20-30 kinds of bagels on the shelves at once, spanning savory to dessert styles, and even labels them by texture grade (T-60 firmer, T-70 softer) so customers can pick the chew they like.
Originally on Kitaoji-dori, Browny moved to its current Shogoin location in 2016, settling into a small storefront near Heian Shrine and Kyoto Zoo.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: dmatcha confirms the 20-30 rotating bagel varieties, the T-60/T-70 firmness grades, domestic wheat with long fermentation, and flavors including gorgonzola-honey-walnut, kinako-mochi red bean, sweet-potato cream cheese and cinnamon-apple-walnut; kyotopi confirms the 2016 move from Kitaoji to Shogoin near Heian Shrine.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Dedicated wheat bakery making bagels, bread and focaccia from domestic wheat; gluten is pervasive throughout the kitchen and there are no gluten-free items, so this is unsafe for celiac diners.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: At least one variety is a soy-sauce mochi cheese bagel; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and no wheat-free soy sauce is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Many bagels and breads are made and baked alongside cheese, cream cheese, honey and dairy varieties on shared equipment, so vegan items are prepared in the same kitchen as animal-product items. Ask staff which specific bagels are egg-free and dairy-free.

positives.text: A HappyCow vegan-bakery directory entry notes a domestic-wheat bakeshop whose main products are bagels, white bread and focaccia, many of which are vegan-friendly, and that it offers soy milk for drinks.
Everything is baked fresh on site and the small storefront is known for friendly service.

cultural_comfort.note: A small neighborhood Japanese bakery with a takeaway counter; staff are described as friendly, but menus and bagel labels are mostly in Japanese, so a few basic Japanese phrases help when asking which bagels are egg- and dairy-free.

vm_gohan_pan_kobo_tsubutsub.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The rice bread is cooked rice kneaded together with wheat flour (Hokkaido wheat), so all breads contain wheat/gluten.
vm_gohan_pan_kobo_tsubutsub.vegan_detail: Rice-bread bakery whose dough kneads freshly cooked Kyoto-blend rice into wheat flour. The base bread is plant-based, using soy milk and rice oil instead of eggs and dairy, and many items contain no eggs, dairy, or honey. Items with animal products are clearly labeled, so vegan diners can select safe options. Not all-vegan, as some products contain eggs, dairy, and honey.
vm_gohan_pan_kobo_tsubutsub.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] Gohan Pan Kobo Tsubutsubu grew out of a rice shop (Okui Riso Mai-ten) and opened after debuting at the Kamigamo Shrine handmade market in summer 2012. The owners knead freshly cooked, just-polished Kyoto-blend rice into the dough with a mochi-pounding machine

chef_bio.background: Gohan Pan Kobo Tsubutsubu is tied to the rice shop Okui Riso Mai-ten (奥井理想米店), which handles its sales, and it debuted at the Kamigamo Shrine handmade market in summer 2012. The bakers knead freshly cooked, just-polished Kyoto-blend rice into the dough with a mochi-pounding machine rather than using rice flour.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name Tsubutsubu references ryuryu-shinku (粒粒辛苦), honoring the grain-by-grain effort of farmers and the value of every grain of rice; the shop emphasizes domestic rice and food self-sufficiency, using Hokkaido wheat chosen to avoid post-harvest pesticides.
chef_bio.specialty: Chewy, fluffy gohan pan (rice bread) made by mixing cooked rice with wheat flour for a naturally sweet, mochi-like texture; many varieties use soy milk and rice oil instead of eggs and dairy.

anecdotes.text: The bread is made from actual cooked rice pounded into the wheat dough, not rice flour, which gives its signature mochi-mochi texture and gentle sweetness.
The business began as a stall at the Kamigamo Shrine handmade market in summer 2012 and still appears at Kyoto handmade markets monthly.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site confirms that the bakery uses freshly cooked Kyoto-blend rice (not rice flour) pounded into the dough, Hokkaido wheat chosen to avoid post-harvest pesticides, soy milk and rice oil in place of eggs and dairy, the ryuryu-shinku name meaning, and that Okui Riso Mai-ten handles sales.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Not gluten-free: every bread is made with wheat flour (rice is kneaded in alongside the wheat), so gluten is present throughout the kitchen.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The facility also produces items containing eggs, dairy, peanuts, and honey, so there is cross-contamination risk for strictly plant-based diners.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Breads containing eggs or dairy are clearly labeled, helping customers avoid animal products and choose plant-based alternatives.

positives.text: The base bread is plant-based, using soy milk and rice oil instead of eggs and dairy; many items are free of eggs, dairy, and honey.
Listed on a vegan/ethical directory as a bakery with many egg-, dairy-, and honey-free items that welcomes plant-based customers.

cultural_comfort.note: Vegan-friendly spot; many such places in Kyoto are used to international visitors.

vm_cafe_frosch.gf_detail: No gluten-free menu or options are documented. The café's identity centers on house-baked bread made with whole-grain wheat flour and natural koji yeast, so wheat/gluten is pervasive in the kitchen. There is no information confirming wheat-free soy sauce or any gluten-free preparation. A celiac or gluten-sensitive diner should treat this as not gluten-safe and ask directly before ordering.
vm_cafe_frosch.vegan_detail: This is an omnivore café (it serves a German sausage sandwich and dishes that may contain dairy/eggs), but it offers a clear set of dedicated vegan options. Reported vegan items include a vegan aubergine (eggplant) burger set served with soup, side, salad and pickles; koji-bread plates with a vegan soup option; an onigiri rice-ball vegan set; and a "little bread" set with vegan soup and salad. The house bread is risen German-sourdough style using koji (a plant-based fermentation culture), and is described as entirely plant-based. Some vegetarian dishes contain dairy or eggs but can often be modified by removing animal products. Staff explicitly recommend telling them your vegetarian/vegan needs and any allergies so they can guide your order.
vm_cafe_frosch.hours_raw: 11:00–17:00; closed Thursdays and Fridays (per official/Tabelog listing; HappyCow lists Thu plus 2nd Friday). Available for private reservations after 17:00 on request. Koji bread baked in-house and sold on Wednesdays and Sundays.
vm_cafe_frosch.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] Café Frosch opened on May 1, 2009, in Kyoto's historic Nishijin textile district, in a renovated traditional machiya (wooden townhouse) that sits within a still-active weaving neighborhood and looks out over a small park. It is set about three minutes east of

chef_bio.background: Café Frosch opened on May 1, 2009, in Kyoto's historic Nishijin textile district, in a renovated traditional machiya (wooden townhouse) about three minutes east of the east gate of Kitano Tenmangu shrine. It was created by two sisters to bring cultural exchange to the historic neighborhood.
chef_bio.philosophy: The café describes itself as a place 'without boundaries' — a space where people of any nationality or age can freely come together to enjoy culture and art. It emphasizes natural ingredients, locally grown Kyoto vegetables, and naturally fermented bread, and welcomes plant-based diners.
chef_bio.specialty: House-baked bread made with whole-grain flour and natural koji yeast — koji bread, bagels, and fig-walnut bread — alongside vegan plates such as a vegan aubergine burger set, koji-bread plates with vegan soup, and an onigiri vegan set. Bread is baked in-house and sold on Wednesdays and Sundays.

anecdotes.text: The café was created as a borderless gathering place for cultural and artistic exchange, hosting events such as English nights, live performances and workshops, and offering rental space.
HappyCow describes it as a café created by two sisters in the historic Nishijin area, combining cultural exchange with vegan-friendly dining and a bakery selling bread on Wednesdays and Sundays.
Its signature bread is risen German-sourdough style using koji, a plant-based fermentation culture, and is made with whole-grain flour and natural yeast.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The café's own Japanese about page confirms the May 1 2009 opening in a Nishijin machiya three minutes east of Kitano Tenmangu's east gate, the borderless culture-and-art concept, and koji bread of whole-grain flour and natural yeast sold Wednesdays and Sundays; HappyCow confirms the two-sister founding and the vegan menu.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The kitchen is bread-focused, baking with whole-grain wheat flour and koji yeast, so wheat/gluten is pervasive; no gluten-free preparation or separation is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is an omnivore kitchen that also serves meat dishes such as a German sausage sandwich, so vegan items are prepared in a shared kitchen; no dedicated vegan-only prep area is documented.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Staff recommend that you tell them about your vegetarian/vegan needs and any potential allergies before choosing a menu so they can guide your order, and some vegetarian dishes can be modified to remove dairy/eggs.

positives.text: Offers a clearly defined set of vegan dishes — a vegan aubergine burger set, vegan koji-bread and onigiri sets — with plant-based, naturally fermented bread.
Reviewers praise the vegan meals as 'fantastic' with thoughtful meal combinations.

cultural_comfort.note: Founded as a borderless cultural-exchange café with international staff who prepare weekend global dishes, and it hosts English nights, so a foreign student should feel comfortable communicating in English.

vm_omen_nippon_shijo_pontoc.gf_detail: This is a wheat-udon restaurant — the signature noodles are made from Japanese wheat flour and are not gluten-free. The dipping sauce/tare and any soy sauce used are conventional (wheat-containing); no wheat-free soy sauce or gluten-free noodle option was found. Tempura batter also contains wheat. Celiac/strict GF travelers cannot eat the core dishes here.
vm_omen_nippon_shijo_pontoc.vegan_detail: Omen is an omnivore udon house, but it maintains a dedicated vegan/vegetarian menu available on request. The plant-based set comes with a vegan dashi (fish-free, kelp/vegetable-based dipping broth) instead of the standard bonito dashi, an assortment of fresh and pickled seasonal Kyoto vegetables, ground sesame, and egg-free vegetable tempura. Omen was noted as one of the first noodle shops to explicitly offer a fish-free (vegetarian) dashi. You must ask for the vegan/vegetarian version when ordering, since the default menu is not plant-based.
vm_omen_nippon_shijo_pontoc.hours_raw: 11:00-16:00 (L.O. 15:00), 17:00-21:00 (L.O. 20:00). Closed 2nd and 3rd Thursdays of the month. (Source: Tabelog. Note: HappyCow lists Wed closed / slightly earlier evening close — hours may vary; confirm before visiting.)
vm_omen_nippon_shijo_pontoc.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] Omen is one of Kyoto's most beloved udon institutions, with its flagship shop near Ginkaku-ji (the Silver Pavilion) on the Philosopher's Path. The name 'Omen' is an honorific dialect word from eastern Japan meaning 'noodles' (men/麺). This Shijo Pontocho branch

chef_bio.background: Omen is one of Kyoto's most beloved udon institutions, with its flagship shop near Ginkaku-ji (the Silver Pavilion) on the Philosopher's Path. The name 'Omen' combines the honorific 'o' with 'men' (麺, noodles). This Shijo Pontocho branch, branded Omen NIPPON, brings the same udon to central Kyoto just off the lively Pontocho lane.
chef_bio.philosophy: A focus on seasonal Kyoto vegetables and quality domestic wheat, presenting udon as an elegant, vegetable-forward meal rather than a quick noodle bowl.
chef_bio.specialty: Thick, chewy udon made from Japanese wheat, served hot or cold with a dipping tsuyu and a generous spread of seasonal Kyoto vegetables (boiled and pickled) plus freshly ground sesame. The house tsuyu is a fish (bonito-and-kombu) broth; for plant-based diners the kitchen prepares, on request, a vegan version with a fish-free vegetable/kelp dashi and egg-free vegetable tempura.

anecdotes.text: Omen NIPPON keeps a separate vegetarian menu: on request the kitchen prepares a vegan udon with a fish-free vegetable/kelp dashi and vegan (egg-free) vegetable tempura, which reviewers single out for its broth and tempura.

The signature 'omen' set pairs hot or cold udon with a colorful assortment of seasonal Kyoto vegetables such as daikon, gobo, eggplant, greens, ginger and scallions, plus ground sesame to stir into the broth.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Omen.co.jp confirms the Ginkaku-ji flagship and a house broth of Hokkaido kombu and bonito; HappyCow confirms that the Omen NIPPON Pontocho branch offers a request-only vegan udon with a fish-free dashi and egg-free vegetable tempura. The standard broth is fish-based, so the vegan version must be requested.

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a wheat-udon kitchen; the noodles, tempura batter and standard tare all contain wheat, so there is heavy gluten presence throughout. No gluten-free preparation or separate handling was described — not suitable for celiac diners.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No wheat-free soy sauce or tamari was mentioned; the dipping sauce/seasonings should be assumed to contain wheat-based soy sauce.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The vegan set uses a separately prepared vegan dashi and egg-free tempura, but the kitchen also handles meat and seafood (e.g., prawn tempura). One reviewer reported being mistakenly served the non-vegan version with prawns, so confirm your order.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Vegan/vegetarian orders are accommodated on request with a distinct broth and sides, and an English menu is available, but plant-based is not the default and at least one order mix-up has been reported — communicate your needs clearly.

positives.text: A dedicated vegan/vegetarian set is available with a fish-free (kelp/vegetable) dashi, fresh and pickled seasonal vegetables, ground sesame and egg-free vegetable tempura.
English menu and staff experienced with international visitors make it easy to request the vegan option.

cultural_comfort.note: There is an English menu and the staff are used to international visitors, so a foreign student can order the vegan set comfortably in English — just clearly request the vegetarian/vegan version.

vm_indo_shokudo_tadka_tadka.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is documented. South Indian cooking here is largely rice- and lentil-based (rice meals, dosa, sambar, rasam, chutney), which is naturally wheat-free, but breads such as roti/parotta contain wheat and asafoetida (hing) used in many dishes is often wheat-cut. There is no published information on dedicated GF prep, soy-sauce contents, or dashi. A celiac/GF traveler must ask directly about each dish.
vm_indo_shokudo_tadka_tadka.vegan_detail: The standard/default lunch menu at TADKA1 is vegetarian (South Indian "Meals"), and the kitchen will prepare vegan versions on request ("定番メニューがベジタリアンで、ヴィーガン対応もしてもらえます"). The VEG MEALS set (around 9 dishes made "with beans and vegetables only") and a SIMPLE VEG SET are vegetable/legume based. Because South Indian vegetarian cooking commonly uses ghee, yogurt, paneer and dairy, vegan diners should explicitly ask for dairy-free preparation. No published per-dish ghee/dairy breakdown was found, so confirm in person or via Instagram (@indosyokudo_tadka).
vm_indo_shokudo_tadka_tadka.hours_raw: Tue-Thu 12:00-16:00 (L.O. 15:30); Fri-Sat 08:00-10:00 (breakfast/dosa) and 12:00-16:00 (L.O. 15:30); Sun & Mon closed
vm_indo_shokudo_tadka_tadka.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan/vegetarian] TADKA's Japanese owner-chef trained at Mughal, a long-established Indian restaurant in Kyoto, before opening TADKA1 in January 2012 as a street-stall-style South Indian lunch spot on Oshikoji-dori. A second, more refined dinner location, TADKA2, followed in De

chef_bio.origin: From Aichi Prefecture, Japan; based in Kyoto
chef_bio.background: TADKA's owner-chef, Dai Okonogi (小此木 大), originally from Aichi Prefecture, trained at Mughal, a long-established Indian restaurant in Kyoto, before opening TADKA1 in 2012 as a street-stall-style South Indian lunch spot on Oshikoji-dori. A second, more refined dinner location, TADKA2, followed in December 2021 nearby.
chef_bio.philosophy: The chef travels to India annually to experience regional cooking in homes, temples, street stalls, cafeterias and restaurants, and prizes the 'diversity' of how a single dish changes by region and context. Spice blends are custom-mixed per curry rather than built on a standardized base, and menus rotate daily with what is seasonal and available.
chef_bio.specialty: South Indian 'Meals' (thali-style vegetable set meals) served with rasam, sambar and chutney; weekend morning dosa/tiffin service.

anecdotes.text: TADKA was awarded a Bib Gourmand in the Indian-cuisine category of the Michelin Guide Kyoto 2023.
Roughly three times a year, for South Indian festivals such as Pongal, Vishu and Onam, TADKA serves an all-vegetarian Sadya of about 20 dishes on a banana leaf.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Japanese listings (search-ethnic, Tabelog) identify the owner-chef as 小此木 大 (Dai Okonogi), from Aichi, who trained at the Kyoto Indian restaurant Mughal before opening TADKA in 2012; the official site confirms TADKA1 (Oshikoji-dori lunch) and TADKA2 (Dec 2021 dinner) plus the annual India travel and the ~20-dish banana-leaf Sadya; the Michelin Kyoto 2023 Bib Gourmand is confirmed by Japanese Michelin round-ups.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen also prepares non-vegetarian dishes (especially at the TADKA2 dinner location), so shared cookware/cross-contact is possible; vegan diners should specify dairy-free and meat-free preparation.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Reviewers report the standard menu is vegetarian and that the kitchen will accommodate vegan requests when asked, but no formal allergy protocol is published.

positives.text: The standard daily VEG MEALS set is built from beans and vegetables only (about 9 items), making it an easy, largely plant-based default.
Much of the South Indian repertoire (rice, sambar, rasam, chutney) is naturally wheat-free and based on rice and lentils.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual lunch counter popular with international diners and listed in English-language guides, so basic Japanese helps but you can get by with a few words and pointing at the vegetarian meals set.

vm_yuba_ryori_higashiyama_y.gf_detail: No gluten-free claims are published. Soy sauce (very likely standard wheat-containing) appears in dishes such as the egg-yolk soy sauce yuba rice, and tempura/fried items and seasonings may contain wheat. Yuba and tofu-milk dishes themselves are naturally wheat-free, but cross-use of regular soy sauce and the lack of any stated gluten protocol means a celiac/GF diner must ask directly and cannot assume safety.
vm_yuba_ryori_higashiyama_y.vegan_detail: This is an omnivore restaurant built around house-made yuba (tofu skin), which is itself plant-based. Many signature elements are vegetable- and soy-forward: the "tofu milk hot pot" with Kyoto vegetables, fresh raw yuba, and yuba-based dishes. However, the kaiseki courses are NOT vegan — they incorporate Miyama-raised Kyoto jidori chicken, free-range egg (e.g. yuba rice topped with egg-yolk soy sauce), and very likely fish-based dashi in soups and seasonings. There is no published dedicated vegan or vegetarian course. A vegan or vegetarian diner would need to phone ahead (075-532-1019) and request a plant-only arrangement; the restaurant explicitly asks for advance notice of allergies and dietary needs, so accommodation may be possible but is not guaranteed. Treat as "ask."
vm_yuba_ryori_higashiyama_y.hours_raw: Breakfast 9:00-10:15 (LO 9:30), Lunch 11:00-15:00 (LO 14:00), Dinner 16:00-22:00 (Mon from 17:30; entry until 20:30, food LO 21:00, drinks LO 21:30). Tue: no dinner service. Closed Thursday (official site also lists Monday closed; schedules differ, so confirm before visiting).
vm_yuba_ryori_higashiyama_y.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] The restaurant is the direct-run dining room of 京・美山ゆば ゆう豆, a yuba (tofu skin) maker based in the mountain village of Miyama in Nantan, northern Kyoto — described as 'the inner sanctum of Kyoto,' about 90 minutes from Kyoto Station near the headwaters of the Y

chef_bio.background: The restaurant is the direct-run dining room of 京・美山ゆば ゆう豆, a yuba (tofu skin) maker based in the mountain village of Miyama in Nantan, northern Kyoto — described as 'the inner sanctum of Kyoto,' about 90 minutes by car from Kyoto Station near the headwaters of the Yura River. The story begins not with cooking but with farming: the company grows its own soybeans and works with neighboring Nantan, Kyoto-north and Tanba growers, using exclusively domestic, Kyoto-centered soybeans (including Tamba black soybeans for its rare black yuba). In 2015 they opened this Gion-Higashiyama restaurant so guests could taste their mountain-made yuba directly.
chef_bio.philosophy: Artisanal craft over efficiency: the makers deliberately produce yuba only 'to the point where it genuinely tastes best eaten fresh,' adjusting daily to temperature, humidity and bean quality by feel rather than machine standardization, and refusing anti-foaming agents (消泡剤未使用) for a concentrated, umami-rich result.
chef_bio.specialty: House-made Miyama yuba served fresh; signature dishes include a soy-milk hot pot with colourful Kyoto vegetables and 'yuba meshi' (yuba rice). Courses are built around the maker's own additive-free yuba, presented as a Japanese-Western fusion kaiseki.

anecdotes.text: The brand supplies its handmade, additive-free Miyama yuba to high-end Kyoto restaurants and hotels, and opened the Higashiyama dining room in 2015 to let the public experience it firsthand.

Evening service offers three kaiseki courses named for the neighbourhood — 'Higashiyama,' 'Gion' and 'Yasaka' — using Miyama yuba, Kyoto soybeans and Miyama water alongside seasonal Miyama and Tanba ingredients.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The maker's site miyamayuba.com confirms the Miyama/Nantan base ~90 min from Kyoto Station, use of only domestic Kyoto-centered soybeans (Tamba black for black yuba), the no-anti-foaming-agent method, and the 2015 Higashiyama restaurant. Hitosara/search confirm the Higashiyama/Gion/Yasaka evening kaiseki courses using Miyama yuba, Kyoto soybeans and Miyama water.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes such as the yuba rice topped with egg-yolk soy sauce indicate standard (wheat-based) soy sauce is used in seasoning; no wheat-free soy sauce is advertised.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is an omnivore kitchen: courses include Kyoto jidori chicken and free-range egg, so plant-based dishes are prepared in a kitchen that also handles animal products. Fish dashi is also likely in soups. Vegan diners should request a fully plant-based arrangement in advance.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The restaurant requests advance notice of allergies and dietary requirements at the time of reservation, suggesting some willingness to accommodate, though no formal vegan/GF protocol is published.

positives.text: The kitchen centers on house-made, additive-free yuba and a tofu-milk hot pot with Kyoto vegetables — plant-based, soy-forward dishes that form a strong vegetarian-friendly base if animal garnishes (egg, chicken, dashi) are omitted on request.

cultural_comfort.note: A refined Gion kaiseki-style spot popular with international visitors via online reservation platforms; some English support and tourist familiarity exist, but a few words of Japanese and a phoned-ahead dietary request will help, especially for vegan/allergy needs.

vm_izusen_sagano.gf_detail: Not gluten-friendly. Wheat-based soy sauce and fu (wheat gluten) are essential, core ingredients in Izusen's cooking and cannot be modified, per InsideKyoto. Tempura batter and other course components also typically contain wheat flour. A celiac or strictly gluten-free diner should not rely on this restaurant; there is no dedicated GF menu or accommodation noted.
vm_izusen_sagano.vegan_detail: Izusen serves shojin ryori (Buddhist temple vegetarian cuisine) that is entirely plant-based, with no meat or fish. As traditional shojin, it also excludes the five pungent vegetables (onion, garlic, etc.). The signature is "teppatsu shojin ryori" — a multi-course set served in stacked red-lacquer iron bowls, featuring seasonal vegetables, sesame tofu (goma-dofu), tofu fritters, vegetable tempura, simmered and vinegared dishes, and matcha with Japanese sweets to finish. Set menus (Ran ¥2,600, Hana ¥3,300, Housenka ¥3,500, Ayame ¥3,800) change with the season. Note: authentic shojin does not use fish or katsuo dashi — broth is plant-based (kombu/shiitake) — but confirm directly if you have a strict requirement.
vm_izusen_sagano.hours_raw: 11:00-16:00; closed Tuesdays (open if Tuesday is a national holiday)
vm_izusen_sagano.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan/vegetarian] Izusen (泉仙) is a long-established Kyoto purveyor of shojin ryori — Buddhist Zen temple vegetarian cuisine — with roots in the city's monastic catering tradition. The Sagano branch sits in the historic Sagano/Toriimoto district near Arashiyama, in a refined woo

roles: Sagano/Arashiyama branch of the Izusen company
chef_bio.background: Izusen (泉仙) is a long-established Kyoto purveyor of shojin ryori — Buddhist Zen temple vegetarian cuisine — with roots in the city's monastic catering tradition. The Sagano branch sits in the historic Sagano/Toriimoto district near Arashiyama and serves the same teppatsu (iron-bowl) shojin style for which the company is known across its Kyoto locations (including its temple branch at Daiji-in within the Daitoku-ji complex).
chef_bio.philosophy: Rooted in Zen Buddhist practice, the food is entirely plant-based, seasonal, and prepared with the shojin ethos of simplicity, gratitude, and non-killing — eating in harmony with nature and the temple calendar.
chef_bio.specialty: Teppatsu shojin ryori — a course meal served in a set of nested red-lacquer (朱塗り) bowls (typically seven, graded large to small) modeled on the teppatsu, the iron alms bowl monks historically carried to receive offerings. Signature items include sticky, nutty sesame tofu (goma-dofu), tofu fritters, vegetable tempura (shojin-age) such as shiitake, and simmered and vinegared/dressed seasonal vegetables, finished with matcha and a Japanese sweet.

anecdotes.text: Meals are served in stacked, luminous red-lacquer bowls and the menu shifts with the seasons — bamboo shoots and asparagus in spring, mushrooms and gingko/chestnuts in autumn — reflecting shojin cuisine's deep tie to the temple year.

The 'teppatsu' presentation uses bowls modeled on the iron alms bowl (鉄鉢) that Buddhist monks historically carried to receive food offerings, tying the modern dining experience to centuries-old monastic practice; the Sagano branch layers original shojin dishes across large-and-small nested bowls.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyoto-izusen.com (Sagano and kodawari pages) and Japanese search confirm 精進鉄鉢料理 served in 朱塗り (red-lacquer) bowls modeled on the monk's iron alms bowl (鉄鉢), with goma-dofu, shojin-age, simmered and dressed vegetables in fucha-ryori style. Inside Kyoto corroborates the seasonal menu and signature sesame tofu/shiitake tempura.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat is structurally central to the cuisine (soy sauce and fu/wheat gluten are core ingredients; tempura uses wheat batter), so gluten is present throughout the kitchen and cross-contamination is effectively unavoidable for a GF diner.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Soy sauce used here is conventional wheat-containing soy sauce and is described as essential to Izusen's cooking and not modifiable.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is a fully shojin (Buddhist vegetarian) operation serving no meat or fish, which greatly reduces the risk of animal cross-contact.

positives.text: Entirely plant-based shojin ryori — no meat, no fish — so vegan and vegetarian diners can eat the standard set menus without modification.
Traditional shojin excludes the five pungent alliums (onion, garlic, etc.), helpful for diners avoiding those.

cultural_comfort.note: A traditional, tourist-frequented shojin spot in Sagano where set courses make ordering simple; basic Japanese greetings help, but the fixed vegetarian menus mean little language is needed to dine comfortably.

vm_taro_bakery.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The bakery's identity is built on domestic (Hokkaido) wheat and natural-yeast wheat bread, so wheat is in essentially everything and the kitchen handles flour throughout. No dedicated gluten-free or wheat-free line was confirmed by reliable sources. Celiac and gluten-sensitive diners should treat this as unsafe.
vm_taro_bakery.vegan_detail: This is an omnivore bakery, but plant-based options are a core part of what they make. The base/plain bread (and a number of the daily loaves) is genuinely vegan: it is made from just four ingredients — Hokkaido domestic wheat, natural (wild) yeast, salt and water — with no butter, vegetable oil, milk, eggs or sugar, slow-fermented 15–18 hours. The owners say they put out "egg-free, dairy-free, sugar-free" items every day specifically for vegans and people with allergies. Seasonal sandwiches use pesticide-free Ukyo-grown vegetables (burdock, lotus root, shiitake, onion), but note that other pastries/sweets on the shelf may contain dairy/egg, so ask which specific items are plant-based on the day.
vm_taro_bakery.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] Taro Bakery is run by Hideyasu Kito and his wife Sumiko. Kito trained as a bread craftsman in Aichi Prefecture, developed a love for honest, simple bread, and chose Kyoto to open his own shop in Tokiwa, Ukyo Ward (the shop opened in 2005).

chef_bio.background: Taro Bakery is run by Hideyasu Kito and his wife Sumiko. Kito trained as a bread craftsman in his native Aichi Prefecture, developed a love for honest, simple bread, and chose Kyoto to open his own shop in Tokiwa, Ukyo Ward (the shop opened around 2005).
chef_bio.philosophy: The couple's ethos is to use ingredients that are 'as delicious and as safe as possible.' They deliberately bake in small batches across many varieties so customers don't tire of the lineup, and they make a point of offering egg-free, dairy-free and sugar-free items every day for vegans and people with allergies.
chef_bio.specialty: Long-fermented natural-yeast loaves made with domestic Hokkaido wheat. The signature plain pain de mie and country breads (campagne) are built from just wheat, wild yeast, salt and water, slow-fermented 15–18 hours for a deep, simple flavor; seasonal sandwiches use pesticide-free vegetables grown locally in Ukyo.

anecdotes.text: The base plain bread is intentionally stripped to four ingredients — Hokkaido wheat, natural yeast, salt and water — with no butter, oil, milk, eggs or sugar, fermented 15–18 hours from the night before.
The shop has a cozy zakka-style (general-store) feel, and the owner's mother's hand-knitted items are sold alongside the bread, miso and preserves.
Sandwiches feature pesticide-free, organically grown vegetables from the surrounding Ukyo area — burdock, lotus root, shiitake and onion.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: digistyle-kyoto (2018) confirms baker Hideyasu Kito trained in native Aichi and opened ~13 years earlier (~2005) in Tokiwa, Ukyo Ward, with wife Sumiko; the 'as delicious and safe as possible' motto; deliberate small-batch variety (少量多種); daily egg/dairy/sugar-free breads; the four-ingredient Hokkaido-wheat loaf fermented 15–18 hours; and pesticide-free Ukyo vegetables in sandwiches.

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a wheat bakery: domestic wheat flour is used throughout and is handled across the whole kitchen, so flour cross-contact is unavoidable. Not suitable for celiac or gluten-sensitive diners.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegan loaves are baked in the same kitchen as breads that contain dairy/egg, so shared-equipment cross-contact is possible. Ask staff which specific items are fully plant-based that day.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The owners deliberately put out egg-free, dairy-free and sugar-free items every day for vegans and people with allergies, indicating allergy awareness — though communication is in Japanese.

positives.text: The plain/base bread is genuinely vegan, made from only Hokkaido wheat, natural yeast, salt and water — no butter, oil, milk, egg or sugar.
Emphasis on safe, simple ingredients and locally grown pesticide-free vegetables in the sandwiches.

cultural_comfort.note: A small neighborhood bakery run by a Japanese family; staff are warm but service is in Japanese, so a few polite phrases and pointing at the loaves will carry you a long way.

vm_yume_ya.gf_detail: The defining draw per the VegeMap listing is "gluten- and dairy-free doughnuts," so at least the doughnuts are made gluten-free. This is not a confirmed fully-dedicated gluten-free kitchen, and there is no information on cross-contamination controls, shared equipment, or whether other items contain wheat. Celiac diners should confirm preparation directly with staff.
vm_yume_ya.vegan_detail: Listed by Japan VegeMap as offering vegan option(s). The standout item is gluten- and dairy-free doughnuts paired with house-roasted coffee, which suggests plant-based-friendly baked goods. However, the VegeMap listing carries no menu detail and is flagged by VegeMap itself as unverified, so exactly which items are fully vegan (no eggs/honey) is not confirmed. A diner should tell staff their requirements and confirm each item before ordering.
vm_yume_ya.hours_raw: Not published on the available source.

chef_bio.background: Yume-ya (written 夢屋, 'coffee shop 夢屋') is a small kissaten-style coffee and bake shop at 116 Yaoya-chō, Nakagyō-ku, Kyoto, in the Rokkaku-dōri / Teramachi arcade area. It operates roughly 10:30-18:00 and is typically closed Mondays (open on public holidays). Alongside coffee it serves house-made baked goods including doughnuts, scones and mini brownies, offered as part of lunch sets. Published listings confirm the address, hours and menu but do not name the proprietor or give a founding date.
chef_bio.specialty: Coffee with house-made bakes: doughnuts, scones and brownies (including a rice-flour baked-doughnut set), served in lunch sets.

anecdotes.text: Lunch sets pair drip coffee with a rotating selection of small house baked goods (doughnuts, scones, mini brownies).

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Japanese shop directories (always.fan, tabelog, kyotodekuraso donut roundup, Retty) confirm the Nakagyō-ku address (八百屋町116), ~10:30–18:00 hours, Monday closures (open on holidays), and the coffee-plus-baked-goods menu, but contain no owner biography or founding date.

staff_allergy_handling.text: VegeMap advises informing staff about dietary requirements before ordering, as the listing is unverified and offerings may differ from what is shown.

positives.text: The shop's signature offering is described as gluten- and dairy-free doughnuts alongside house-roasted coffee, indicating a deliberate focus on gluten-free and dairy-free baking.

cultural_comfort.note: A small Kyoto coffee-and-doughnut spot; basic Japanese or pointing will help, and a friendly "konnichiwa" plus showing your dietary needs should be enough for a quick takeaway order.

vm_hakko_shokudo_kamoshika_.gf_detail: No gluten-free menu or GF information is published. The kitchen's seasonings center on traditional Japanese fermented products — soy sauce (醤油), miso, and amazake. Their dressing ingredient list includes soy sauce, and standard Japanese shoyu and most miso contain wheat, so dishes should be assumed to contain gluten unless confirmed. Rice and many pickles are naturally gluten-free, but cross-use of wheat-containing soy sauce/miso is likely. A celiac/gluten-sensitive diner must ask directly; safety cannot be assumed.
vm_hakko_shokudo_kamoshika_.vegan_detail: Not a vegan restaurant. The flagship dish, the "8-kinds fermented set meal" (発酵8種定食), contains fish: mackerel heshiko, pufferfish pickled in rice bran, and konjac dressed with fish sauce. However the kitchen leans heavily on plant-based fermentation, so vegan/plant-based choices exist: koji-natto served in/over deep-fried tofu, fermented vegetable pickles (nukazuke), white-miso soup, and salads dressed with their house brown-rice amazake dressing (explicitly labeled vegan/植物性: brown-rice amazake, rapeseed oil, onion, vinegar, soy sauce, sugar, plum, salt). A vegan diner should ask staff to omit the fish/fish-sauce components of the set or order plant-based items à la carte. White miso soup may use dashi — confirm it is kombu-based and not bonito.
vm_hakko_shokudo_kamoshika_.hours_raw: Tuesday–Saturday 11:30–17:00 (lunch service until 15:00; 15:00–17:00 light meals/café). Closed Sunday and Monday. Reservations recommended during the lunch rush.

chef_bio.background: Founded in May 2014 in Saga-Arashiyama, Kamoshika is a restaurant-and-shop devoted to fermented food, opened by Megumi Seki. The name カモシカ comes from 醸し家 (kamoshi-ya, 'brewing house'), reflecting the in-house fermentation. It pairs a ground-floor dining room with a 2nd-floor 'Fermentation Marché' (発酵マルシェ) selling house-made and nationwide fermented goods, plus DIY fermentation kits and online workshops.
chef_bio.philosophy: Their motto is 'returning fermented foods to the kitchen' (発酵食を台所に取り戻す) and proposing a '発酵のある暮らし' (a life with fermentation), emphasizing health, flavor, and sustainability through traditional, additive-free fermented seasonings.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature 発酵8種定食 (8-kinds fermented set meal), in which everything but the rice is fermented — including koji-natto, nukazuke pickles, white-miso soup, and Awa-bancha fermented tea. Popular plant-based items include koji-natto over deep-fried tofu and salads with house brown-rice amazake dressing.

anecdotes.text: The shop name カモシカ is a play on 醸し家 ('brewing house'), reflecting that the food is fermented (醸す) on-site under its all-fermentation theme.
Beyond dining, Kamoshika runs a 2nd-floor Fermentation Marché and online fermentation workshops, treating fermentation as a whole lifestyle rather than just a meal.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: co-trip and kamoshika.kyoto.jp confirm founder Seki Megumi (関恵), the May 2014 Saga-Arashiyama opening, the 醸し家 → カモシカ name origin, the 1F dining / 2F 発酵マルシェ structure with online workshops, and the 発酵8種定食 in which everything but the rice is fermented (koji-natto, nukazuke, white-miso soup, Awa-bancha tea).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Traditional Japanese soy sauce and miso (core to this kitchen) typically contain wheat; no GF accommodation is published, so gluten cross-contact via seasonings should be assumed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The house brown-rice amazake dressing ingredient list includes 醤油 (soy sauce); there is no indication it is a wheat-free tamari, so it should be assumed to contain wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is an omnivore kitchen: the signature set meal includes mackerel heshiko, pufferfish nukazuke, and fish-sauce konjac, so fish is handled in the same kitchen as plant-based dishes. White miso soup may use a fish (bonito) dashi — confirm it is kombu-only.

positives.text: Strong focus on traditional, additive-free fermented seasonings (naturally brewed soy sauce, miso, mirin, house-made koji and brown-rice amazake), and clearly identified vegan/plant-based items such as the brown-rice amazake dressing, koji-natto with fried tofu, and vegetable nukazuke.

cultural_comfort.note: An official English website exists, but it's a small traditional fermented-food restaurant; a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu will help when asking to omit the fish components or to check for wheat/dashi.

vm_orto.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is documented. The menu is course-based and bread/pasta feature heavily (e.g. shiitake bread, grilled negi bread, maitake pasta), so wheat is prevalent. The restaurant asks guests to declare all allergies and dislikes in advance of the visit (it cannot accommodate requests after arrival), which means a gluten-free adaptation would have to be negotiated when reserving. Whether soy sauce is wheat-free and whether any dashi is used in the vegan course are not stated — confirm directly. Treat GF as ask/by-arrangement only.
vm_orto.vegan_detail: ORTO is an omnivore innovative restaurant (its standard tasting course features fish, octopus, duck and house-made bacon) but it offers a dedicated, fully vegan multi-course menu and a separate vegetarian course — one of the few high-end Kyoto restaurants with a genuine 100% vegan set course. The kitchen defines vegan as no meat, fish, shellfish, dairy, eggs or honey. The cooking centers on seasonal Kyoto vegetables (kyoyasai), edible flowers and herbs, with restrained salt and oil. Per VegeMap, vegan reservations are accepted at lunch only and must be arranged in advance — you cannot order the vegan course on the spot. Always reserve the vegan/vegetarian course ahead and state your needs clearly when booking.
vm_orto.hours_raw: Mon, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun & public holidays 18:00-22:00; closed Tue & Wed. (Vegan course reservations noted as lunch/noon only by VegeMap — confirm when booking.)
vm_orto.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] Owner-chef Shinji Tanimura grew up surrounded by Kyoto's famous vegetables (kyoyasai). After culinary school he trained in Italian cuisine, then rediscovered the power of vegetables while cooking at a French restaurant. At 31 he traveled to Italy before return

chef_bio.origin: Born 1976 in Kumiyama, just south of Kyoto
chef_bio.background: Owner-chef Shinji Tanimura grew up surrounded by Kyoto's famous vegetables (kyoyasai). After culinary school he trained in Italian cuisine, then rediscovered the power of vegetables while cooking at a French restaurant. At 31 he traveled to Italy before returning home to open ORTO in central Kyoto in August 2008. In March 2016 he reworked the restaurant around its 'vegetable garden' identity.
chef_bio.philosophy: 'ORTO' is Italian for 'vegetable garden.' Tanimura cooks to let seasonal ingredients breathe, deliberately restraining salt and oil so the natural strength of each vegetable comes through all five senses, transcending the boundaries of any single cuisine.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal Kyoto-vegetable course cuisine blending Italian and French technique. Signature plant-forward dishes include a 'garden' (菜園) salad of around 30 vegetables, herbs and edible flowers, and house-baked breads such as grilled negi (leek) bread, alongside seasonal vegetable-led pastas. Beyond the omnivore tasting menu, ORTO is one of very few Kyoto restaurants offering dedicated vegetarian and full vegan multi-course menus.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant dropped 'Ristorante' from its signage, signaling a deliberate move beyond traditional Italian boundaries into genre-transcending, vegetable-led cuisine.

After the 2016 renovation the 'vegetable garden' concept became central, and ORTO began offering dedicated vegetarian and vegan menus so diners could experience the quality of Kyoto vegetables through all five senses.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: italianweek100 confirms chef Tanimura was born 1976 in Kumiyama, trained in Italian then French cuisine (where he rediscovered vegetables), went to Italy at 31, opened ORTO in Aug 2008, and renovated in March 2016 dropping 'Ristorante' to focus on seasonal Kyoto vegetables with reduced salt/oil and dedicated vegetarian/vegan menus. takemachelin corroborates the ~30-vegetable garden salad and in-house negi bread.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Bread and pasta are core to the menu (shiitake/negi breads, maitake pasta), so wheat and gluten are heavily present in the kitchen; no gluten-free protocol is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is an omnivore kitchen whose standard course includes fish, octopus, duck and house-made bacon, so animal ingredients are handled alongside the vegan course; the vegan menu is prepared to order rather than in a separate animal-free kitchen.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The restaurant asks guests to inform them of all allergies and dislikes in advance and states it cannot accommodate requests made after arrival — so any dietary needs must be arranged at the time of reservation.
The kitchen offers a true 100% vegan course and defines vegan strictly as no meat, fish, shellfish, dairy, eggs or honey, indicating clear understanding of plant-based requirements.

positives.text: One of the few high-end Kyoto restaurants offering a genuine full vegan multi-course menu built around seasonal Kyoto vegetables, herbs and edible flowers.
Because the vegan course is reserved and prepared individually in advance, the chef can plan a fully animal-free plate rather than improvising on arrival.

cultural_comfort.note: A refined reservation-only course restaurant that appears in English vegan guides and takes online bookings; a little Japanese or a clearly-worded advance reservation stating your vegan needs will make the experience smooth.

vm_kerala.gf_detail: No dedicated gluten-free program documented. Rice dishes (saffron/basmati rice) and rice-flour dosas are naturally wheat-free, but naan, papad, pakora batter and some curry thickeners may contain wheat, and shared cookware means cross-contact is likely. No information on dedicated fryers or wheat-free soy sauce. A GF-sensitive or celiac diner must ask staff directly about each dish.
vm_kerala.vegan_detail: Omnivore Indian restaurant with a strong vegetable focus rooted in Kerala/Ayurvedic cuisine, offering many plant-based choices. Reviewers report a range of vegan-adaptable dishes: tofu curry, chana masala, aloo gobi, dal, vegetable pakoras, and masala dosa. Vegan items are not labeled on the menu, but English-speaking staff can advise which dishes can be made vegan by omitting dairy and eggs (and confirm whether chutneys/accompaniments are vegan). Naan and many breads contain wheat; the soybean/lotus-root curry and rice-based dosas are good plant-based picks. Confirm ghee, cream (used in some curries), and dairy in breads when ordering.
vm_kerala.hours_raw: Tue-Sun: Lunch 11:30-14:00, Dinner 17:00-22:00 (L.O. 21:00). Closed Monday. Some guides note irregular closures.
vm_kerala.notes: [VegeMap-sourced · vegan options] Kerala is one of downtown Kyoto's longstanding Indian restaurants, tucked on the second floor of the KUS Building just north of Kawaramachi-Sanjo. It is named for the South Indian state of Kerala, the birthplace of Ayurveda, and serves both South and North Ind

chef_bio.background: Kerala is one of downtown Kyoto's longstanding Indian restaurants, tucked on the second floor of the KUS Building just north of Kawaramachi-Sanjo. It is named for the South Indian state of Kerala, the birthplace of Ayurveda, and serves both South and North Indian cooking from a famously compact, corridor-like dining room decorated with Indian furnishings.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen leans on Kerala and Ayurvedic ideas of light, vegetable-rich, easy-to-digest food, which gives plant-based diners an unusually wide field of choices for a non-vegetarian Indian restaurant; most vegetarian dishes can be made vegan on request by asking for no dairy or egg.
chef_bio.specialty: Crispy rice-based dosas (the masala dosa is a favourite) and an extensive curry menu (often described as 40-plus varieties), with vegetable-forward options like chana masala, aloo gobi and dal. The house tomato (and cream) soup is a signature, and the good-value lunch sets pair curries with saffron rice and bread.

anecdotes.text: Guides describe the space as little more than a cramped corridor lined with tables, yet praise it as one of the best places downtown to take a break from Japanese food while shopping.
The restaurant frames its menu around Ayurvedic principles from Kerala state, offering healthy, vegetable-abundant dishes that are light and easy to digest.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: k021500.gorp confirms the restaurant is named for Kerala state (birthplace of Ayurveda), serves authentic South Indian cooking with 40-plus curries, and that tomato-cream soup is a top seller (28 seats total). HappyCow reviews confirm both South and North Indian dishes, dosas (masala dosa), chana masala/aloo gobi/dal, and that most vegetarian dishes can be made vegan on request. Inside Kyoto confirms the 2F KUS Building location and cramped-corridor space.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No gluten-free program is documented; naan, papad and fried items share a kitchen with wheat, so a wheat-sensitive diner should ask before ordering.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is an omnivore Indian kitchen that also serves meat and dairy dishes; many curries use cream or ghee, so vegan diners should request no dairy/eggs and confirm each dish.

staff_allergy_handling.text: English-speaking staff can tell which dishes can be made vegan and will confirm whether dips and accompaniments like chutneys are dairy/egg-free.

positives.text: A wide range of vegetable-based and adaptable plant dishes (tofu/soybean curry, chana masala, aloo gobi, dal, vegetable pakoras, masala dosa), with staff used to advising vegan diners.
Vegetable-forward, Ayurveda-inspired menu makes plant-based ordering easier than at a typical non-vegetarian Indian restaurant.

chef_bio.background: Pippara is a famously tiny (about 10-seat) home-style Indian/Nepalese curry counter tucked down an alley by the Kyoto University Faculty of Agriculture, where it has long been a gathering spot for students. Open only Friday through Sunday, it serves an all-in set plate of several curries with turmeric rice, freshly baked chapati, a fried snack and a small lassi for an unusually low price (around 780 yen).
chef_bio.philosophy: The name comes from pippala (Sanskrit for the bodhi/sacred fig tree under which the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment), framing the little shop as a place for seekers, fitting for its university crowd. The owner runs it with deliberate, almost monastic house rules: greet loudly on entry, wait for your order to be taken, order decisively, eat cleanly and finish within about 60 minutes.
chef_bio.specialty: An all-in-one multi-curry set plate: typically several curries that rotate daily (including a chana/legume curry and a fish option), served with turmeric rice, freshly griddled chapati and a fried snack.

anecdotes.text: The name Pippara derives from the bodhi (pippala) tree under which the Buddha attained enlightenment, casting the shop as a meeting place ('the bodhi tree where Kyoto University students gather').

The proprietor is known for strict but affectionate house rules; in one anecdote she scolded a regular who asked for a bigger lassi — not for asking, but for not noticing she had already poured him an extra-large one as a service ('I always give you the large one without asking! Don't you understand?').
The shop is a set-meal place for people who order quickly, eat cleanly, and don't linger (within about 60 minutes).

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The ameblo report confirms the pippala/bodhi-tree name and the 'bodhi tree where Kyoto U students gather' framing, ~10 seats, Fri–Sun opening, the ~780-yen all-in set (curries + turmeric rice + chapati + fried snack + small lassi), the lassi-scolding anecdote, and the ~60-minute rule; search corroborates the strict entry etiquette (greet, wait for the order to be taken, order '一通り').

gf_cross_contamination.text: Freshly baked chapati (wheat) is part of the standard set and fried snacks use batter, so wheat is handled openly in the kitchen; no gluten-free accommodation is indicated.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Vegetarian options are explicitly available, but the owner runs a fast, no-reservations counter with strict house rules and limited time per customer, so make any vegan/allergy requests quickly and clearly.

positives.text: Vegetarian options are confirmed available, and the daily plate already includes multiple plant-based vegetable and legume curries (e.g. potato-tomato and chana/chickpea), giving a vegetarian or flexible-vegan diner real choices.
Curries are described as light, home-style and gentle on the body rather than heavy, with an inexpensive all-in set plate.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, quirky student-favorite counter run by a famously strict but caring owner who expects a polite greeting, a quick decision, clean eating and leaving within about 60 minutes — a few words of Japanese and good manners go a long way, so come ready to order promptly.

chef_bio.background: Hanbei-Fu was founded in 1689 (Genroku 2) by Tamaoki Hanbei and has handcrafted Kyoto fu (wheat gluten) and yuba (tofu skin) for over three centuries, at the south-east corner of the Kawabata-Gojo intersection by the Gojo Ohashi bridge, overlooking the Kamo River. Within its machiya complex, a Showa-era building (designed by architect Ryo Tanahashi) houses the tea house, Sabo Hanbei.
chef_bio.philosophy: Fu and yuba were introduced to Japan by Zen monks, and the house's cooking belongs to the shojin ryori (Buddhist vegetarian) lineage, centered on plant-based proteins and respect for water, ingredients and craftsmanship.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature offering is the 'Mushiyashinai' course (むしやしない / 虫養い), a Kyoto-dialect name for a light meal that gently staves off hunger, showcasing an array of fu and yuba dishes.

anecdotes.text: The signature yuba-and-fu course is called 'Mushiyashinai' — a Kyoto word (虫養い) for a light bite that gently nourishes the stomach.
Fu is made from wheat flour mixed with water, kneaded and washed to remove the starch, and was brought to Japan by Zen monks as part of shojin ryori.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kanpai-japan and hanbey.co.jp confirm the 1689 founding by Tamaoki Hanbei, the 300-plus-year fu/yuba craft, the location at the SE corner of Kawabata-Gojo by Gojo Ohashi over the Kamo River, the Showa-era building (by architect Ryo Tanahashi) housing the Sabo Hanbei tea house, fu as wheat gluten introduced by Zen monks, and the 'Mushiyashinai' course. (The romanization was corrected from 'Mushi Yoinai.')

gf_cross_contamination.text: The entire menu is built around fu, which is concentrated wheat gluten, so the kitchen is inherently wheat-heavy and not suitable for gluten-avoidant or celiac diners.

positives.text: Core dishes are plant-based fu (wheat gluten) and yuba (tofu skin) in the shojin vegetarian tradition, so the menu is largely free of meat and fish.

cultural_comfort.note: Vegan-friendly spot; many such places in Kyoto are used to international visitors.

Futomaki and tamago-maki contain egg and are not vegan. There is no published confirmation of whether the sushi rice/vinegar, pickled radish, or rolls use animal- or wheat-free seasonings, so a strict vegan should ask directly. chef_bio.background: Sushizen is a long-established Kyoto sushi shop that opened as a sushi restaurant in 1939 (Showa 14), having started as a fish shop, on Sanjo-dori (Shinmachi) in the Karasuma-Oike area of Nakagyo-ku. It has served the same neighborhood for generations, long loved by local families.
chef_bio.philosophy: An everyday, good-value neighborhood shop rather than a high-end counter; the rice is given a sharper vinegared edge to balance the toppings, a deliberate Kyoto take on chirashi.
chef_bio.specialty: Its signature is a colorful chirashi sushi: a mound of golden shredded egg crepe (kinshi-tamago) blanketing seafood — tuna, sea bream, amberjack, grilled anago, octopus and squid — over seasoned rice, finished with a house sweet sauce. It also offers nigiri, futomaki, and Kyoto-style pressed (hako-zushi/oshi) sushi.

anecdotes.text: Recognized in the MICHELIN Guide as a Bib Gourmand selection (since the 2023 Kyoto & Osaka guide) for good-quality, good-value cooking.
The most popular item is the seafood chirashi (around 1,700–1,850 yen), topped with shredded egg crepe over an abundant bed of fish, finished with a house sweet sauce.

The Michelin Guide lists it as a Bib Gourmand selection (first in the 2023 Kyoto & Osaka guide).

chef_bio.background: QUÉ PASA started because its owner missed the burritos eaten constantly while a student in the United States. After graduating from a Japanese university and moving to Kyoto to help with the family's bok choy (pak choi) wholesale business, the owner began selling burritos despite having no prior restaurant experience, self-teaching through YouTube and customer feedback.
chef_bio.philosophy: To create a casual, come-anytime place where anyone can get a consistently delicious meal whether grabbing a quick bite or gathering with friends, faithfully recreating authentic American-Mexican burrito flavors in Kyoto.
chef_bio.specialty: Generously sized California-style burritos and tacos, with vegetable-forward and made-to-order vegan versions (including custom tofu and shiitake burritos).

anecdotes.text: The shop reopened in April 2024 at the same Kawaramachi-Kojinguchi spot after the building was rebuilt, keeping its relaxed American-diner atmosphere that draws many international visitors.
The owner is happy to accommodate vegans, having created off-menu items like tofu and shiitake burritos on request, and runs an all-vegan menu about once a month.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Leaf Kyoto (Japanese lifestyle magazine) confirms the owner studied in the U.S., missed burritos there, and after helping the family pak-choi wholesale business opened QUÉ PASA with no restaurant background, refining recipes via YouTube and customer feedback; it reopened April 2024 after the building was rebuilt at the Kawaramachi area (荒神口/Kōjinguchi) location.

chef_bio.background: The Maeda story begins in the soil. After more than 35 years cooking — including training in Italy at fine-dining and Michelin-starred kitchens — Takamitsu Maeda turned toward organic, plant-forward food. He launched an organic online shop in 2007, took on farmland in Nantan, Kyoto in 2009 to grow his own vegetables, and opened the vegan restaurant Organic House Salute near Kyoto Station in 2013. da Maeda is his organic Italian table set inside a roughly 110-year-old renovated Kyoto townhouse (machiya), where the vegetables he farms become wood-fired pizza, pasta, and plant-based plates.
chef_bio.philosophy: A circular, soil-to-soil ethos: 'starting with soil cultivation, through farming and dining, and returning to the soil.' Food should be kind to the body and to the planet, built on organic and naturally-farmed ingredients sourced from the chef's own land and like-minded producers across Japan.
chef_bio.specialty: Organic Italian cooking from the chef's own farm, with standout vegan plates such as a breaded soy cutlet in almond-caper sauce, a soy patty in porcini red-wine demiglace, chickpea croquettes, and wood-fired vegetable pizza.

anecdotes.text: In 2019 Maeda opened a sister concept at the same machiya — Lapis, a fully-vegan sushi kaiseki served entirely by reservation, where a 15-course plant-based meal is plated on antique Japanese dishes and lacquerware.
In 2021 he created WAoWA, billed as Japan's first trademark-registered fermented coffee brand, extending the fermentation-and-circulation theme that runs through the kitchen.
A guest singled out the breaded soy cutlet with almond-caper sauce as surprisingly rich and satisfying — substantial enough that they wished for a larger portion.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: da-maeda.com and its Lapis page confirm Maeda's 30+/35-year cooking career with Michelin-starred Italian training, the 2007 organic online shop, 2009 Nantan farmland, 2013 Organic House Salute, the ~110-year-old machiya, the 2019 reservation-only 15-course vegan sushi kaiseki 'Lapis' served on antique dishes, and the 2021 WAoWA fermented coffee (described as Japan's first trademark-registered fermented coffee), all under a 'soil-to-soil' circular philosophy.

chef_bio.background: Bean's Goody is a small cafe set inside a renovated traditional Kyoto townhouse (machiya) in the Kinugasa neighborhood of Kita Ward, near Kinkaku-ji. It opened in August 2015 and is built entirely around one unusual specialty: black bean coffee (黒豆珈琲), a caffeine-free brew made from roasted Tanba black soybeans rather than coffee beans.
chef_bio.philosophy: The cafe centers on making a gentle, caffeine-free black bean coffee accessible while preserving its quality, and on showcasing local Tanba black soybeans. The owner has publicly expressed gratitude to longtime patrons for their steady support ('これも、変わらず支えていただいた皆様のおかげです').
chef_bio.specialty: Caffeine-free black bean coffee made from Kyoto Tanba black soybeans, plus black bean jelly and black bean coffee jelly; light fare includes a vegetable burger and 'dog-style' sandwiches.

anecdotes.text: The black bean coffee is naturally caffeine-free, and after brewing, the spent black beans can be reused to make black bean tea, so guests can taste both from the same beans.
The cafe has hosted art fairs and events where it sold its black bean coffee drip bags alongside vegan baked goods from Seiun Oyatsu (星雲おやつ), which use no animal-derived ingredients.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: beans-goody.com confirms the Kinugasa/Kita-ku machiya cafe opened August 2015 around caffeine-free black bean coffee (黒豆珈琲) from Tanba black soybeans, black bean and coffee jellies, a vegetable burger and 'dog' sandwiches, the reuse of spent beans for black bean tea, and the owner's published thanks to loyal patrons ('これも、変わらず支えていただいた皆様のおかげです').

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is an omnivore kitchen serving ham & cheese, tuna and egg sandwiches alongside its plant-based items, so cross-contact with animal products is possible for vegan diners; confirm preparation when ordering.

positives.text: The signature black bean coffee is made purely from Tanba black soybeans, is caffeine-free and inherently plant-based and gluten-free, and soy milk is available as a dairy alternative for cafe au lait.
The cafe offers a vegetable burger and has stocked fully vegan baked goods (Seiun Oyatsu) made without animal-derived ingredients.

cultural_comfort.note: A small local machiya cafe near Kinkaku-ji where a little Japanese helps; staff are welcoming, but menus and explanations are primarily in Japanese, so learning to ask "Is this vegan?" (これはヴィーガンですか) is useful.

chef_bio.background: The Ritz-Carlton, Kyoto opened in 2014 on the west bank of the Kamogawa river at the Nijo-Ohashi bridge, designed around a contemporary Japanese aesthetic and traditional garden setting in central Kyoto. Its dining portfolio spans an Italian restaurant (La Locanda), a cluster of Japanese counters under the Mizuki name (kaiseki, sushi, tempura, teppanyaki), a lobby lounge, a bar, a chef's table, and a Pierre Hermé Paris boutique.
chef_bio.philosophy: Hospitality built around personalized service, including accommodating dietary preferences such as vegan, vegetarian and gluten-free when guests notify staff.
chef_bio.specialty: Refined Italian cuisine using local Kyoto produce at La Locanda, and multi-discipline Japanese fine dining at Mizuki; afternoon tea in the riverside Lobby Lounge.

anecdotes.text: La Locanda's menu explicitly flags dishes as (VG) vegan, (GF) gluten-free and (LF) lactose-free, making plant-based and allergen choices identifiable rather than guesswork (guests are still asked to notify staff of any allergies).
The hotel sources a 100% gluten-free amazake granola made locally in Kyoto for its breakfast service, a small sign of attentiveness to gluten-free guests.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official La Locanda menu page confirms the (VG) vegan / (GF) gluten-free / (LF) lactose-free notation (and an allergy-notification request); the Ritz-Carlton dining materials and independent reviews confirm the 2014 opening on the Kamogawa at Nijo-Ohashi, the La Locanda / Mizuki / Pierre Hermé line-up, and the 100%-gluten-free Kyoto-made amazake granola at breakfast.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Guests are asked to inform their server of any food allergies or vegetarian/vegan needs so the kitchen can accommodate them; allergy disclosure before ordering is part of the standard service.

chef_bio.background: Owner Nakagawa opened the restaurant around 2014 out of a love for Okinawan and pan-Asian cooking, settling in the Jodoji neighborhood near Kyoto University. The name plays on goya (bitter melon) and Goya/Koza, the Okinawan city seen as the birthplace of 'chample' (mix-it-all-together) culture.
chef_bio.philosophy: Nakagawa aims for a '食籍なき食卓' - a 'food-passport-free table' where vegans, vegetarians and meat-eaters can all sit and eat together. He didn't set out to build a vegan menu; it grew naturally as he responded to requests from the foreign residents and international students in the neighborhood, reflecting Okinawa's blended Chinese-Japanese-American 'chample' spirit.
chef_bio.specialty: Okinawan 'chample' dishes given a vegan-friendly twist - vegan taco rice with soy meat and avocado in place of cheese, Nasi Campur seasonal vegetable plates with Okinawan seaweed and Kume-island miso soup, goya champuru, island-tofu dishes, and vegan banana tarte.

anecdotes.text: The vegan menu wasn't planned - Nakagawa kept saying yes to requests from international students and foreign residents near Kyoto University until plant-based dishes naturally became a large part of the offering.
He notes that Okinawan ingredients have such strong flavor that even non-vegetarians enjoy the veg dishes ('沖縄食材は味がしっかりしているので、ベジじゃない方にも喜ばれてます').
Reviewers describe a cozy, authentic wooden machiya setting with very friendly staff; one diner was sent off with complimentary Okinawan chopsticks.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Vegewel's interview confirms owner Nakagawa opened around 2014 in Jodoji near Kyoto University, the goya/Goya-Koza chample naming, the '食籍なき食卓' (food-passport-free table) ethos, the organic growth of the vegan menu from international residents' requests, signature vegan taco rice (soy meat + avocado, no cheese), Nasi Campur, Kume-island miso soup and island tofu, and the quote that strongly-flavored Okinawan ingredients please non-vegetarians too.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No information is published on whether the soy sauce used is wheat-free; standard Japanese shoyu typically contains wheat. Confirm directly if avoiding gluten.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Meat-based Okinawan dishes are prepared in the same kitchen, so a fully vegan order should be requested explicitly.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Staff routinely ask diners whether cheese, egg or dashi are acceptable, showing solid awareness of vegan and vegetarian dietary needs when taking orders.
English-speaking staff and an English menu make it easier to communicate dietary restrictions.

positives.text: Vegan dishes are clearly marked on the menu, so plant-based diners can choose confidently.
Staff proactively confirm dashi/egg/cheese, which is a strong allergy-awareness signal for an omnivore restaurant.

cultural_comfort.note: English-speaking staff and an English menu are available, and the place is used to international students and travelers, so a foreign student can order vegan items comfortably in English.

chef_bio.background: A vegetable-focused dining bar ("yasai dining") in central Kyoto, just off Kawaramachi-dori south of Sanjo. The restaurant builds its menu around seasonal Kyoto heirloom vegetables - Shogoin daikon and turnip, Horikawa burdock, Kujo green onions, Kyoto carrots - alongside rare produce sourced from farmers across Japan, paired with wine.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name 薬師 (Kusushi), an old Japanese word for a physician/healer, captures the owner's ethos that vegetables are medicine: the goal is to help guests eat many kinds of vegetables and become healthier, using only safe, traceable produce from farmers whose faces they know.
chef_bio.specialty: Dishes that put unusual and seasonal vegetables front and center: a 20-vegetable salad, Kujo-negi and burdock kinpira pizza, and Inca-potato tomato-cheese bakes, plus a rotating lineup of rare vegetables from around the country.

anecdotes.text: The shop is named after 薬師 (kusushi), an archaic word for a doctor, reflecting the belief that eating a wide variety of vegetables makes you healthier.
Vegetables are chosen for safety and trust - sourced from across Japan where 'the farmer's face is visible,' with a focus on Kyoto heirloom varieties.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The shop's own site (kdh9700.gorp.jp) confirms the 薬師/kusushi name (archaic word for a doctor) and 'vegetables are medicine' ethos, sourcing safe produce from farmers 'whose faces are visible' with a focus on Kyoto heirloom vegetables (Shogoin daikon, Horikawa burdock, Kujo negi), plus a 20-vegetable salad, Kujo-negi/burdock kinpira pizza and Inca-potato tomato-cheese bake, on the 3rd floor near Kawaramachi south of Sanjo.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is an omnivore izakaya, not a vegan kitchen: the regular menu includes dairy (cheese bakes, cheese-topped pizza) and the kitchen handles meat and fish, so a vegan order shares equipment and surfaces with animal products. Vegan dishes are prepared only on advance request, so cross-contact handling depends entirely on arranging this ahead.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The vegan map listing states vegan service is available 'by advance reservation,' implying the kitchen will tailor a plant-based course if you call ahead (075-212-4313) - but no formal allergen or gluten protocol is published.

positives.text: The whole concept is vegetable-forward, so plant-based diners have a genuinely large palette of seasonal Kyoto and nationwide vegetables to draw from when a vegan course is arranged in advance.

cultural_comfort.note: A local Kyoto izakaya with primarily Japanese-language service and menu; a foreign diner can manage with a few Japanese phrases, and a vegan should phone ahead (basic Japanese helpful) to arrange a plant-based course.
