chef_bio.origin: Kyoto (originally a yatai stall in Kiyamachi, now Shijo-Kawaramachi)
chef_bio.background: Menya Yukou began as a humble yatai (street food stall) called 屋台優光 in Kyoto's Kiyamachi district before relocating to a permanent storefront in the heart of the city at Shijo-Kawaramachi, just south of Takashimaya and beside Good Nature Station. The owner trained at the renowned Osaka ramen shop 人類みな麺類 (Jinrui Mina Menrui) before striking out on his own. The Kawaramachi shop opened on September 23, 2021, and is the flagship of a small group that also runs 麺屋聖~kiyo~, a shop devoted to spreading Kyoto's dashi culture.
chef_bio.philosophy: Built around Kyoto's dashi culture and freshly made noodles - the team makes noodles fresh each morning and leans on carefully blended Kyoto soy sauces to keep the broths clean and delicate rather than heavy.
chef_bio.specialty: A light, refined shellfish-dashi shoyu ramen (貝らーめん) that condenses the umami of oyster, clam and shijimi over a base of blended Kyoto soy sauces - a shellfish-broth style that is relatively rare in Kyoto. The shop is equally known for its rich duck-dashi tsukemen (鴨つけ麺), a group-first creation limited to roughly 15 bowls a day, and a Kyoto-style shoyu ramen layered with bonito, kombu and meat umami. A torched rare-chashu rice bowl (炙りレア焼豚丼) is a favorite side.

anecdotes.text: The shop grew from a single Kiyamachi yatai (street stall) called 屋台優光 into a permanent Shijo-Kawaramachi storefront, with the owner having trained at Osaka's celebrated 人類みな麺類.
Designed to feel more like a cafe than a typical ramen shop, the interior plays Mr. Children throughout service and explicitly welcomes solo diners, including women.
The duck-dashi tsukemen was a first for the Yukou group and is limited to around 15 servings per day.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 公式(yukou-kiyo.com)・osumituki・takemachelinより、木屋町の屋台優光から四条河原町(高島屋南2軒)へ移転、2021年9月23日開業、店主は人類みな麺類出身。貝らーめん(牡蠣・あさり・しじみ)を京都醤油で、鴨つけ麺は一日15食限定、炙りレア焼豚丼、カフェ風でミスチルが流れる店内を確認。

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Broths and tare are built on blended Kyoto soy sauces, which in Japan are standardly brewed with wheat; combined with wheat ramen noodles this makes the bowls unsuitable for celiacs.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broths are animal-based (shellfish dashi, duck/bonito/kombu, meat-enriched shoyu) and bowls carry pork chashu and egg, so there is no plant-based separation.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, welcoming counter ramen shop in a busy central tourist area; a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu go a long way, and solo diners (including women) are explicitly welcomed.

kyr_no_ko_kyo_tori_paitan_ra.gf_detail: This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop. The bowls use standard wheat ramen noodles and a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare in the black version, both of which contain wheat. No gluten-free noodles, dedicated prep, or allergen accommodation are mentioned by any source. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_no_ko_kyo_tori_paitan_ra.vegan_detail: The entire concept is a chicken-based broth (tori-paitan), simmered for hours from domestic chicken and aromatic vegetables, with toppings of chicken chashu and chicken tsukune (meatballs). There is no plant-based broth or vegan bowl. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kyr_no_ko_kyo_tori_paitan_ra.hours_raw: Mon-Thu 11:00-22:30 (L.O. 22:00); Fri-Sat 11:00-23:30 (L.O. 23:00); Sun 11:00-17:00 (L.O. 16:30). Open year-round (sources vary slightly on exact open/close times).
kyr_no_ko_kyo_tori_paitan_ra.notes: [Mom & Pop] Opened in 2015 in the Shijo-Karasuma area of central Kyoto, Menya Mitsuru built its reputation on a single idea done well: a rich, collagen-heavy chicken paitan broth. The proprietor came from a mizutaki (chicken hot-pot) specialty background, and that pedigree shows in how the b

chef_bio.background: Opened in 2015 in the Shijo-Karasuma area of central Kyoto, Menya Mitsuru built its reputation on a single idea done well: a rich, collagen-heavy chicken paitan broth. The proprietor came from a mizutaki (chicken hot-pot) specialty background, and that pedigree shows in how the broth is built — fresh domestic chicken simmered in volume over high heat for long hours until it turns creamy and white. Pointedly, the shop uses no pork at all; the depth here is all chicken and aromatics. The shop has since added a sister location in the Gion / Nawate area.
chef_bio.philosophy: Refinement over heaviness — the broth aims to be intensely flavorful yet clean rather than cloying, expressing 'the paitan's original character' in the white version while the black leans into layered umami.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is the 濃厚鶏白湯そば (rich chicken paitan soba), offered in a salt-based 'white' version that showcases the broth's natural character and a soy-tare 'black' version built to amplify umami. There is also a bonito-enhanced 京鰹節鶏白湯 and an extra-rich 超濃厚 version. Bowls come dressed with chicken chashu, chicken tsukune meatballs, kikurage wood-ear mushroom, and scallion, with medium-thick straight noodles chosen to carry the thick broth.

anecdotes.text: The owner previously worked at a mizutaki (chicken hot-pot) specialty restaurant, bringing that refined chicken-broth craft to a ramen format — and deliberately uses only domestic chicken and aromatic vegetables, with no pork in the broth.
The broth is made by simmering large quantities of fresh domestic chicken over high heat for an extended time to draw out a creamy, white paitan.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyoto.tips・kyotopiより、2015年に四条烏丸(中京区)で開業、水炊き専門店出身の店主、豚不使用・国産鶏と香味野菜のみの濃厚鶏白湯(白=塩/黒=醤油)、鰹だし版・超濃厚版、祇園縄手に姉妹店、鶏チャーシュー・つくね・きくらげ・葱、中太ストレート麺を確認。

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The soy-tare 'black' version of the paitan soba is seasoned with shoyu, which is wheat-containing soy sauce.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All bowls are built on a chicken broth with chicken chashu and chicken tsukune toppings; the shared broth and kitchen make any plant-only request unworkable.

cultural_comfort.note: A modern, clean counter-only ramen shop near a major station that draws a broad crowd including solo diners and tourists; a few Japanese greetings go a long way but no special preparation is needed.

kyr_chinyu_kawaramachi_rokka.gf_detail: This is a wheat-noodle chuka-soba shop. The bowl is built on wheat ramen noodles, a soy-sauce tare (Japanese shoyu almost always contains wheat), and a chicken-bone broth — none of it is celiac-safe, and there is no gluten-free menu or noodle option. Not suitable for anyone needing a strict gluten-free meal.
kyr_chinyu_kawaramachi_rokka.vegan_detail: The signature broth is a long-simmered chicken paitan (chicken bones, whole chicken, chicken feet) finished with rendered back fat, and bowls are topped with chashu pork. There are no advertised vegan or vegetarian ramen options. Not a fit for plant-based diners.
kyr_chinyu_kawaramachi_rokka.notes: [Mom & Pop] Chinyu traces back to 1950 (Showa 25), when it began as a single ramen yatai (street stall) wheeled out in a still-recovering postwar Kyoto. The founder eventually set down roots in an eight-tsubo storefront along what would become Ichijoji's famous 'ramen street,' and the house

chef_bio.background: Chinyu traces back to 1950 (Showa 25), when it began as a single ramen yatai (street stall) wheeled out in a still-recovering postwar Kyoto. The founder eventually set down roots in an eight-tsubo storefront along what would become Ichijoji's famous 'ramen street,' and the house is now counted among the wellsprings of the Kyoto chicken-paitan, back-fat style. The Kawaramachi Rokkaku branch carries that lineage into the center of town, on the first floor of the Rokkaku Kaikan just off Shinkyogoku.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's stated creed is plain and stubborn: 奇をてらわない、手を抜かない — no gimmicks, no shortcuts — pouring everything into a single honest bowl while still pushing to refine the craft.
chef_bio.specialty: Chuka-soba (中華そば): a chicken-bone white broth simmered long with whole chicken and chicken feet for a collagen-rich body, mellowed with an aged soy-sauce tare and finished tableside with a generous scatter of fresh back fat. It looks rich but drinks surprisingly clean, and you can dial in noodle firmness, the amount of green onion, and how much back fat you want.

anecdotes.text: The brand's own telling: born in 1950 from a postwar Kyoto street stall, it grew into a tiny eight-tsubo Ichijoji shop and became one of the source points of Kyoto's chicken-broth, back-fat ramen tradition.
Listings highlight the trademark move of the style — fresh back fat scattered over the bowl to order — and a broth that reads heavy by sight but lands light and mellow on the palate.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 公式沿革・ホットペッパーより、1950年(昭和25)に屋台で創業、一乗寺の八坪店に定着、京都の鶏白湯・背脂ラーメンの源流の一つ。『奇をてらわない、手を抜かない』を信条に、丸鶏・鶏足の白湯＋熟成醤油ダレ＋後がけ背脂、河原町六角店は六角会館1Fを確認。

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water and the broth/tare contain wheat-based shoyu; a shared ramen kitchen offers no gluten-free path or separation.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tare is described as an aged/traditional soy sauce ('老舗の醤油でまろやかな風味に'), and Japanese brewed shoyu is almost always made with wheat — treat the seasoning as wheat-containing.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The base broth is chicken paitan (chicken bones, whole chicken, chicken feet) finished with animal back fat, so every bowl is animal-based with no plant-based stock available.

cultural_comfort.note: A roomy, modern, walk-in chuka-soba shop in the central Shinkyogoku/Sanjo tourist zone — easy for a visitor to enter, order at the counter, and slurp a bowl with just a few words of Japanese.

kyr_menjokoro_toritani.gf_detail: This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop. The bowls are built on house-made wheat noodles (medium-thick curly and straight flat-cut varieties) served in chicken broth, with the salt and "thick soy" (shoyu/tare) versions almost certainly using wheat-based soy sauce. There is no indication of any gluten-free noodle, gluten-free tare, or allergen accommodation. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_menjokoro_toritani.vegan_detail: The entire menu is built around chicken — clear chicken broth, concentrated aged chicken paitan, chicken char siu, seared chicken (tataki), and roast-pork butter rice. There are no plant-based broths or vegan bowls. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kyr_menjokoro_toritani.hours_raw: Mon–Fri 11:15–14:30, 18:05–22:00; Sat/Sun/Holidays 11:00–15:00, 18:00–22:00. Closes early when sold out.
kyr_menjokoro_toritani.notes: [Mom & Pop] A refined neighborhood ramen-ya in the Saiin area of Kyoto, set between the Keifuku Yamanouchi and Hankyu Saiin stations. The room has a quiet, almost traditional-Japanese-restaurant feel rather than the look of a typical ramen counter, and it draws steady weekday crowds with lin

chef_bio.background: A refined neighborhood ramen-ya in the Saiin area of Kyoto, set between the Keifuku Yamanouchi and Hankyu Saiin stations. The room has a quiet, almost traditional-Japanese-restaurant feel rather than the look of a typical ramen counter, and it draws steady weekday crowds with lines on weekends despite not sitting on a prime corner.
chef_bio.philosophy: Cooking without chemical seasonings (無化調), leaning on the quality and combination of ingredients, and keeping the kitchen open into the evening (until around 10 PM, later than most local rivals).
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is its chicken soba, offered in two registers: a clear, no-MSG (無化調) tori-soba, and the namesake jukusei (aged) chicken soba — a deeply concentrated, high-viscosity chicken paitan that the kitchen finishes without sweetness, ending on a clean, almost bitter note. The chicken char siu is a standout, praised as approaching proper chicken cookery in its own right, and the kitchen's confidence with chicken extends to seared tataki preparations.

anecdotes.text: House-made noodles — a medium-thick, slightly chewy curly noodle and a straight flat-cut version with firm, mochi-like bite — are matched to the broths so they grip the concentrated soup.
A small side of butter rice with chicken and roast pork (around 300 yen) is singled out as punching well above a typical side dish.
The chicken char siu is described as exceptional, 'reaching the realm of chicken cuisine itself.'

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi・noodlersより、西院(右京区)、和食店のような静かな佇まい、無化調・清湯系、鶏そばと熟成鶏白湯の二本立て(白湯は甘さを抑え後味やや苦め)、『鶏料理の域』と評される鶏チャーシュー・鶏たたき、自家製麺、破格300円の鶏とローストポークのバターごはんを確認。

gf_cross_contamination.text: Ramen here is wheat-noodle based and broths/tare are chicken and (for the soy version) wheat-soy-sauce based; no gluten-free handling is indicated anywhere.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The shoyu ('thick soy' / 鶏そば soy-style) bowls use soy sauce tare, which in a standard Japanese ramen-ya is wheat-based; no wheat-free tare is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broths are chicken-based and toppings include chicken char siu and roast pork; there are no plant-based options, so no meaningful vegan handling exists.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, locals-focused counter ramen shop with no English support expected; ordering is straightforward but basic Japanese or pointing will help most.

kyr_ramen_tsurumusha.gf_detail: This is a chicken-paitan ramen shop built on wheat. Noodles are made in-house daily from a blend of Kyoto-grown "Kyo-komugi" wheat and Hokkaido "Kitahonami"/"Haruyutaka" wheat flours, and the tare/seasoning is shoyu-based (soy sauce, which in Japan is typically brewed with wheat). The broth itself is chicken plus pork bones with aromatic vegetables. There is no indication of any gluten-free noodle, gluten-free tare, or celiac accommodation. Not safe for celiac; a gluten-avoider has essentially nothing safe on the core menu. Confirm directly with the shop if you must, but treat as not gluten-free.
kyr_ramen_tsurumusha.vegan_detail: All bowls are built on an animal broth — whole chicken (from Omi) plus pork bones and aromatic vegetables — and the tare uses kombu, shiitake, and dried scallop (dried scallop is animal-derived). Toppings include pork shoulder rare chashu. There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen on the menu. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kyr_ramen_tsurumusha.hours_raw: Mon/Wed/Sat/Sun: 11:00-14:00, 18:00-21:00. Tue/Thu: 11:30-14:00, 18:00-21:00. Fri: closed. (Lunch and dinner service with a mid-afternoon break.)
kyr_ramen_tsurumusha.notes: [Mom & Pop] Owner-chef Yoshiaki Nishimura was originally a programmer. The birth of his second child became the turning point: he wanted to create a ramen shop that parents could comfortably walk into with kids in tow. He trained at the long-established Kyoto ramen house Chinyu before going

chef_bio.background: Owner-chef Yoshiaki Nishimura was originally a programmer. The birth of his second child became the turning point: he wanted to create a ramen shop that parents could comfortably walk into with kids in tow. He trained at the long-established Kyoto ramen house Chinyu before going independent and opening his own shop in 2012.
chef_bio.philosophy: So the whole family can eat here with peace of mind. To that end the shop uses no preservatives and no chemical seasonings (MSG), and keeps child seats and child cutlery at the counter, with kids openly welcomed.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is a salt-based chicken-paitan (tori-paitan) ramen. The broth is built from whole chicken from Omi plus pork bones and aromatic vegetables, simmered about 30 minutes while the scum is carefully skimmed; the tare is drawn from kombu, shiitake, and dried scallop steeped in water from the day before and slowly cooked down. The result is light on the palate yet creamy and mellow. The rare chashu is pork shoulder seasoned with salt alone to let the meat's own flavor come through, and the house menma is rehydrated over four days then seasoned, never made in advance.

anecdotes.text: The noodles are made fresh every day on the shop's own noodle machine, using a blend of Kyoto-grown Kyo-komugi wheat with Hokkaido Kitahonami and Haruyutaka flours; each portion is hand-massaged and aged into smooth, springy medium-thick wavy noodles.
Nishimura left a programming career to open the shop in 2012 after training at Kyoto's old-guard ramen house Chinyu, specifically wanting a place easy to enter with children.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Amakara Techo profiles Nishimura as an ex-programmer who opened Tsurumusha in 2012 after training at Chinyu, wanting a family-friendly shop; it documents the Omi-chicken shio paitan, the day-ahead kombu/shiitake/scallop tare, the 4-day menma, the Kyo-komugi noodle blend, and the no-preservative/no-MSG child-welcoming policy.

gf_cross_contamination.text: In-house wheat noodles are made daily on the shop's own noodle machine, so the kitchen is a wheat-heavy environment.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The seasoning/tare and items like the house menma are soy-sauce (shoyu) based; Japanese soy sauce is typically brewed with wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broth is animal-based (whole chicken plus pork bones and vegetables) and the tare includes dried scallop; toppings include pork chashu. No vegan/vegetarian option exists.

positives.text: No preservatives and no chemical seasonings (MSG) are used, reflecting an explicit safe-for-the-whole-family ethos.
Child seats and child cutlery are provided and children are actively welcomed.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, family-run neighborhood counter ramen shop that is unusually welcoming to families and newcomers, but expect Japanese-only ordering, so a few polite words and pointing at the menu will carry you through.

kyr_men_au_katajikenai.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering. The signature bowls are wheat ramen noodles (sourced from Kyoto's Teikaku / 麺屋棣鄂) served in chicken-paitan or shellfish broth, and the tare almost certainly uses wheat-based soy sauce. There is no celiac-safe option and no published allergen handling; not suitable for strict gluten avoidance.
kyr_men_au_katajikenai.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly shop. Both signature broths are animal-based — a creamy chicken paitan and a clear shellfish (clam/scallop/oyster) dashi — and toppings include meat. No vegan or vegetarian ramen is offered.
kyr_men_au_katajikenai.hours_raw: Tue–Sun: 11:00–16:00 (L.O. 15:30/15:45) and 17:00–21:00 (L.O. 20:45). Monday: morning ramen service 8:00–10:30 only. (Tabelog also lists a daily 09:00–16:00 / 17:00–21:00 pattern; the morning/asa-ramen slot on Monday and rotating limited bowls mean times can shift.)
kyr_men_au_katajikenai.notes: [Mom & Pop] The shop opened in late August 2023 in the Saiin area of western Kyoto, near Saiin Station. Its chef trained at 鶏soba座銀 (Tori Soba Zagin), a highly regarded Osaka ramen shop, and carries that pedigree into a calm, design-forward counter space with gray finishes and wood furniture

chef_bio.background: The shop opened in late August 2023 in the Saiin area of western Kyoto, near Saiin Station. Its chef trained at 鶏soba座銀 (Tori Soba Zagin), a highly regarded Osaka ramen shop, and carries that pedigree into a calm, design-forward gray-mortar counter space of about nine seats.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name KATAJIKENAI (忝い) means 'grateful / much obliged' — an expression of gratitude that frames the shop's hospitality, paired with a focus on clean, refined broths and quality ingredients.
chef_bio.specialty: A two-style 'twin-broth' lineup: a creamy chicken paitan (鶏白湯そば) whose foamed, emulsified soup is blended just before serving, and a clear shellfish dashi (貝清湯そば) built from Shinji-ko clams, hamaguri, scallops and oysters for a clean oceanic aroma. A daily-limited tsukemen version of the chicken paitan (鶏白湯つけそば) rounds out the menu. Noodles are sourced from Kyoto maker 麺屋棣鄂.

anecdotes.text: The chef trained at the popular Osaka shop 鶏soba座銀 before opening here in August 2023.
The kai-dashi (shellfish) broth is drawn from a mix of Shinji-ko clams, hamaguri, scallops and oysters for a layered seafood umami and an 'aroma of the sea'.
The chicken paitan soup is foamed/emulsified with an immersion blender (bamix) just before service for a light-yet-creamy texture.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyotopi (two articles) covers the Aug-2023 Saiin opening, the chef's 鶏soba座銀 pedigree, the chicken-paitan and shellfish (Shinjiko-clam/hamaguri/scallop/oyster) broths, and the immersion-blender foaming; Tabelog confirms the daily-limited 鶏白湯つけそば tsukemen.

cultural_comfort.note: A small 9-seat counter ramen shop with a ticket-machine order system and cash-only payment, so a few words of Japanese and basic point-and-order etiquette go a long way; staff are unlikely to handle detailed English allergy requests.

kyr_ramen_mugyu_vol_1_honten.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation. This is a classic ramen shop: wheat noodles ("chewy, thick noodles") in a chicken/Nagoya-Cochin broth blended with soy sauce (Japanese shoyu, which contains wheat). The signature bowls (Onibara White/Black, rich chicken soba) and the mazesoba all use wheat noodles, and the soy-sauce tare adds wheat. No celiac-safe option exists here.
kyr_ramen_mugyu_vol_1_honten.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. The broth is built on Nagoya Cochin chicken and chicken bones, and the shop is known above all for its char siu (roasted pork belly) — there are no plant-based ramen options.
kyr_ramen_mugyu_vol_1_honten.hours_raw: 11:00–22:30 (last order 22:00). Closes early when the day's char siu sells out. Official site lists open year-round; some listings note irregular closures, and one review noted a Wednesday closure, so it is best to confirm before a special trip.
kyr_ramen_mugyu_vol_1_honten.notes: [Mom & Pop] Ramen Mugyu opened its Vol.1 main shop in the Enmachi area of Kyoto's Nakagyo Ward in January 2017, just a couple of minutes' walk from JR Enmachi Station. It is a small, glass-fronted counter shop that has grown into a local favorite, since expanding to additional Mugyu branches

chef_bio.background: Ramen Mugyu opened its Vol.1 shop in the Enmachi area of Kyoto's Nakagyo Ward on January 21, 2017, seconds' walk from JR Enmachi Station. Once a branch of an Osaka-Umeda lineage, it became the brand's main shop after the original stores closed, and the Mugyu name has since expanded to further branches around the city.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop sums itself up as '自慢のスープ、こだわりの焼き豚' — pride in the soup and devotion to the char siu. The kitchen leans on quality Nagoya Cochin chicken for a clean, deeply savory base, and a small flourish of minced (rather than sliced) onion adds a crisp texture in place of the usual scallion.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowls are the 'Onibara' series — Onibara White, a clear shio ramen built on a Nagoya Cochin broth blended with light (usukuchi) soy sauce, and Onibara Black, a darker soy version — alongside a richer thick chicken soba (濃厚鶏そば). All are crowned with the shop's celebrated char siu: roasted pork sliced generously over chewy, hand-massaged flat noodles. There is also a mazesoba finished with Nagoya-Cochin chicken oil.

anecdotes.text: The char siu is the shop's calling card — one Kyoto ramen reviewer rated the firm, meaty, fat-controlled roasted pork as their No.1 among Kyoto ramen shops, with four generous slices on a regular bowl.
The Onibara White shio bowl is praised for a clear, clean, refined taste, the Nagoya Cochin broth lifted by a blend of light soy sauce, with minced onion worked into the soup.
A musician credited as YAGI MASAHIKO (pen name X.L.H.) — a producer, composer and guitarist — created a theme song for the Mugyu brand, a quirky touch for a ramen shop.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official Mugyu site gives the brand slogan, the X.L.H. theme song and the branch list; kyoto-gourmet documents the Nagoya-Cochin/light-soy Onibara White, the No.1-rated 4-slice char siu and minced onion; osumituki records the Jan-21-2017 Enmachi opening.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is described as Nagoya Cochin chicken blended with light soy sauce (薄口醤油); Japanese soy sauce is normally brewed with wheat, making the tare a wheat source on top of the wheat noodles.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The broth is built on Nagoya Cochin chicken and chicken bones and the shop centers on roasted pork belly char siu, so all bowls contain animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, casual, popular neighborhood ramen counter where ordering is straightforward; little to no English is expected, so a few Japanese phrases or pointing at the menu helps.

kyr_ramen_so_chikyu_kibo_de__2.gf_detail: This is a Jiro-style ramen shop: the bowl is built on thick wheat noodles in a sweet-soy (wheat shoyu) tonkotsu broth, so it is not celiac-safe. No gluten-free noodles, broth, or accommodations are mentioned anywhere. A celiac diner should not eat here.
kyr_ramen_so_chikyu_kibo_de__2.vegan_detail: A pork-based Jiro-style shop — tonkotsu (pork-bone) broth, pork back-fat (アブラ), char siu, and pork toppings are central to every bowl. No vegan or vegetarian options are mentioned. Not suitable for vegans.
kyr_ramen_so_chikyu_kibo_de__2.hours_raw: Tue/Thu/Sat 11:00-14:45, 18:00-23:45; Wed/Fri 18:00-23:45; Sun 11:00-21:45; Mon closed. (Some listings give the broader window as 11:00-15:00 / 18:00-24:00 weekdays, Sun 11:00-22:00.)
kyr_ramen_so_chikyu_kibo_de__2.notes: [Mom & Pop] Sora is the Saiin branch of the Kyoto Jiro-style chain Ramen-so Chikyu Kibo de Kangaero, which grew out of the group's roots in Kyoto's Fushimi area. This Ukyo Ward location opened on April 24, 2017.

chef_bio.background: Sora is the Saiin branch of the Kyoto Jiro-style chain Ramen-so Chikyu Kibo de Kangaero, which grew out of the group's roots in Kyoto's Fushimi area. This Ukyo Ward location opened on April 24, 2017.
chef_bio.philosophy: Classic inspired-by-Jiro abundance: pile it high, let the diner dial in garlic, vegetables and fat to taste.
chef_bio.specialty: Jiro-style ramen built on thick, chewy house-made noodles (ワシワシとした自家製極太麺) under a towering mound of bean sprouts and cabbage, with char siu, garlic and pork back-fat in a sweet-soy tonkotsu broth. The regular bowl comes with 300g of noodles (a small is 200g), scaling up further for big appetites.

anecdotes.text: Ordering uses the Jiro-style call system, and this chain has its own signature extra-fat call nicknamed 'chomo' that regulars layer onto the standard ニンニク/ヤサイ/アブラ chant — a call that only works at this group's shops.
The Saiin shop opened April 24, 2017 as a branch of the group with roots in Kyoto's Fushimi area.
Even on a rainy day the counter drew about a 40-minute wait, a sign of its local following.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Osumituki records the April-24-2017 Saiin opening and Fushimi-rooted lineage; noodlers.jp documents the house-made 極太 noodles, the 300g-regular/200g-small portioning, the chain-only 'chomo' fat call, and the ~40-minute rainy-day wait.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth/tare is a sweet soy-flavored tonkotsu, which in Jiro-style ramen relies on wheat-containing shoyu; combined with the wheat noodles this bowl is not gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork is fundamental — tonkotsu broth, pork back-fat (アブラ), and char siu — so there is no vegan-safe preparation.

cultural_comfort.note: A cash-only, ticket-machine Jiro-style counter shop run for regulars; you order by calling out toppings in Japanese (ニンニク garlic, ヤサイ vegetables, アブラ fat, カラメ stronger flavor), so a little Japanese and knowing the system helps a lot.

kyr_menhan_shokudo_teradaya.gf_detail: Not gluten-free safe. The core dishes are wheat-noodle chuka-soba and ramen, and the shoyu/soy-based tare and seasonings almost certainly contain wheat. The signature karaage is flour-coated fried chicken. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated fryer, and no celiac accommodation is advertised. A celiac diner cannot eat the ramen here; call ahead (075-432-8878) if you want to ask about anything, but assume cross-contamination throughout a small single-operator kitchen.
kyr_menhan_shokudo_teradaya.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly shop. The broth is built on pork clear soup plus fish/seafood dashi, bowls come with chashu, wonton and egg, and the headline side is fried chicken. There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen option. Vegans should choose a different restaurant.
kyr_menhan_shokudo_teradaya.hours_raw: 11:00–15:00 / 18:00–22:00 (Mon, Tue, Wed, Fri, Sat, Sun). Closed Thursdays plus irregular closures.
kyr_menhan_shokudo_teradaya.notes: [Mom & Pop] Teradaya started life as a wildly popular karaage popup operating out of a shared kitchen (kashikiri / magari) near Kyoto's Sanjo-kai shopping arcade. After the fried chicken built a following, the owner added ramen to the lineup, and on July 1, 2023 the business graduated to its

chef_bio.background: Teradaya started life as a wildly popular karaage popup operating out of a shared kitchen near Kyoto's Sanjo-kai shopping arcade. After the fried chicken built a following, the owner added ramen to the lineup, and on July 1, 2023 the business graduated to its own storefront in the Mibu-Bojo No. 2 housing complex near Shijo-Omiya, rebranding as a sit-down menhan shokudo (a noodle-and-rice diner) while keeping the Teradaya name.
chef_bio.philosophy: A friendly, unpretentious diner doing two things well: a balanced, light-leaning chuka-soba and seriously good fried chicken, with rice bowls and beer to round out a casual meal.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the tokusei chuka-soba: a pork clear broth (chintan) layered with a fish-forward Japanese wafu dashi for a clean, restrained umami, finished with low-hydration, slightly angular noodles prized for a smooth slurp. The 'special' version is a generous spread of extra chashu, three wontons and a soft egg. Alongside it, Teradaya's original soy-garlic karaage — four big, juicy, piping-hot pieces — remains the shop's calling card.

anecdotes.text: The owner has been described, with affection, as looking more like a hip-hop musician than a traditional ramen-ya master.
The karaage is the dish that made the name: four large, soy-garlic-marinated pieces served sizzling and juicy — the kind of plate locals call 'beer-progressing.'

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyotopi documents Teradaya's Sanjo-kai karaage-popup origins, the July-1-2023 move to the Mibu-Bojo No.2 complex near Shijo-Omiya, the tokusei chuka-soba (pork chintan + fish dashi, with extra chashu/3 wontons/soft egg), the 4-piece soy-garlic karaage, and the solo owner's hip-hop look.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen/chuka-soba noodles are the core product, boiled in shared water; the soy-based tare and seasonings almost certainly contain wheat. Not suitable for celiac diners.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Broth/tare is built on soy-based seasoning (chuka-soba shoyu profile), which in Japan is typically brewed with wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is pork clear soup plus fish/seafood dashi; bowls carry chashu, wonton and egg. No vegan options and pervasive animal stock.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual neighborhood noodle-and-rice diner run largely by one operator; little to no English is expected, so a few Japanese phrases or a translation app will smooth ordering.

kyr_gankomen.gf_detail: Not suitable for celiac/gluten-free diners. This is a classic chicken-pork-bone ramen shop: the noodles are wheat (sourced from noodle maker Menya Teigaku / 麺屋棣鄂), and the broths and tare almost certainly use wheat-based soy sauce, especially the 濃厚醤油 (rich soy) bowls. There are no gluten-free options and no indication of allergen handling. Avoid if you have celiac disease.
kyr_gankomen.vegan_detail: No vegan options. Every bowl is built on a chicken-and-pork-bone (とりとんこつ) base, with niboshi (dried sardine) used in the 煮干し variant and pork chashu, pork-fat (背脂) mazesoba, and karaage on the menu. Nothing on the menu is plant-based.
kyr_gankomen.hours_raw: 11:00-14:00 (lunch only); closed Mondays. Note: one local article listed extended evening hours (11:00-14:30 / 17:30-22:00) and "Monday Ganko Men" special events, but the consistent current listing is lunch-only.
kyr_gankomen.notes: [Mom & Pop] 頑固麺 sits in the Fukakusa stretch of Fushimi, one of Kyoto's most competitive ramen districts, a short walk from Fujinomori Station and the Meishin/Route 24 area. The owner is said to have trained at a well-regarded Fushimi-Momoyama ramen shop before striking out on his own, and t

chef_bio.background: 頑固麺 sits in the Fukakusa stretch of Fushimi, one of Kyoto's most competitive ramen districts, a short walk from Fujinomori Station. The owner trained at a well-regarded Fushimi-Momoyama ramen shop before striking out on his own, and the place has become a lunchtime fixture that draws lines even on weekdays despite being open only midday.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's name plays on 頑固 ('stubborn'); the kitchen leans into a single-minded pursuit of a fully-realized, concentrated bowl. A house condiment nicknamed the 'Ganko sauce' is offered as a flavor intensifier so diners can dial the broth up to one of the densest in Kyoto.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is a thick chicken-pork-bone bowl (とりとんこつ): chicken slowly simmered down to a rich, almost paste-thick consistency, with pork umami arriving on the finish, yet kept clean and approachable rather than heavy. It is paired with snappy medium-thin wavy noodles from Kyoto noodle maker Menya Teigaku (麺屋棣鄂), topped with large rare chashu, menma, onion and a hit of mayu (burnt-garlic oil). Variations include 煮干しとりとんこつ (with dried sardine), 濃厚醤油とりとんこつ (rich soy), 鶏中華そば, and a back-fat 背脂 mazesoba.

anecdotes.text: The chef is reported to have trained at a popular Fushimi-Momoyama ramen shop before opening his own counter in the Fukakusa ramen battleground.
The 'Ganko sauce' on the table lets guests intensify the broth into what one guide calls one of Kyoto's most concentrated bowls.
The broth is built by slowly simmering chicken for richness and body, with pork umami lingering in the finish, yet staying clean without off-flavors.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyotopi (g2OHY, RJYMT) covers the Fushimi-Momoyama training, the 'Ganko sauce', the 麺屋棣鄂 medium-thin wavy noodles, and mayu/large-chashu/menma/onion toppings; kyoto-gourmet confirms the chicken-forward tori-tonkotsu broth, the menu variations, and the lunch-only (11:00–14:00) hours near Fujinomori Station.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are the base of every bowl, sourced from noodle maker Menya Teigaku (麺屋棣鄂); shared noodle-boiling water means heavy gluten cross-contact throughout the kitchen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The lineup includes 濃厚醤油とりとんこつ (rich soy chicken-pork-bone) and a 背脂醤油 mazesoba, indicating wheat-based soy tare is used in the broths/seasoning.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All bowls are chicken-and-pork-bone based, with niboshi (dried sardine), pork chashu, back-fat and karaage on the menu; there is no plant-based preparation line.

staff_allergy_handling.text: No allergy information is provided by the shop or in available write-ups.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, ticket-machine ramen counter where lines form at lunch; little to no English is expected, so basic Japanese or pointing at the ticket machine helps.

kyr_mendokoro_janomeya.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The bowls use the shop's own house-made Japanese wheat noodles, and the soy-based (鶏そば) bowls use wheat soy-sauce tare; no gluten-free noodle or dedicated prep is offered. Even the salt/paitan bowls are served with wheat noodles. Avoid if you require strict gluten avoidance.
kyr_mendokoro_janomeya.vegan_detail: This is a chicken specialist — every signature bowl is built on 100% jidori (local chicken) broth made from chicken gara, whole chicken and water, with chicken/duck chashu toppings. There are no vegan or vegetarian ramen options.
kyr_mendokoro_janomeya.notes: [Mom & Pop] The owner came to ramen from fine dining: he started his career in French cuisine and trained at several restaurants before opening his own shop, and he brings those classical kitchen techniques to every bowl.

chef_bio.origin: The shop moved to its current 2nd-floor spot on the narrow Hanayu-koji lane just off Kawaramachi, reopening on December 8, 2020.
chef_bio.background: The owner came to ramen from fine dining: he started his career in French cuisine and trained at several restaurants before opening his own shop, and he brings those classical kitchen techniques to every bowl.
chef_bio.philosophy: Radical simplicity in service of the bird: the broth is built from nothing but chicken bones (gara), whole chicken, and water, letting the flavor of 100% jidori (local heritage chicken) speak for itself. Toppings are charcoal-grilled to add aroma rather than mask the broth.
chef_bio.specialty: Chicken in every form. The two pillars are the 鶏そば — a clear (清湯) chicken broth with a sharp, bright wheat-soy edge and deep chicken-oil richness — and the 鶏白湯, a creamy, concentrated chicken-paitan bowl. A jidori salt bowl rounds out the lineup, all served over house-made Japanese wheat noodles with low-temperature chicken chashu and charcoal-grilled toppings.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen leans on the owner's French-cooking discipline — low-temperature-cooked chicken chashu and charcoal-grilled aromatics show a chef applying restaurant technique to a bowl of ramen.
The house philosophy is summed up as using 'only gara, whole chicken, and water' so the chicken itself carries the flavor.
Reviewers single out the 鶏そば for its balance of bright soy seasoning over a clear chicken broth with real chicken-oil depth, with a side of tori-meshi (chicken rice) as the classic pairing.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Leaf Kyoto describes the owner's French-cuisine background, the 100%-jidori 'gara/whole-chicken/water' broth, low-temp chicken chashu and charcoal-grilled toppings; hikonan-biog reviews the 鶏そば with tori-meshi; osumituki records the Dec-8-2020 reopening on the 2nd floor of Hanayu-koji.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Bowls are served over the shop's own house-made Japanese wheat noodles, so wheat is intrinsic to every dish; there is no gluten-free option.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature 鶏そば is a soy-seasoned (醤油) chicken broth; standard Japanese shoyu tare contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broths are 100% chicken (gara, whole chicken, water) with chicken/duck chashu toppings; there is no meat-free preparation, so any bowl will contain animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A small counter-and-table ramen shop tucked on the 2nd floor of a narrow shopping lane; ordering is straightforward but basic Japanese (or a translation app) helps, and it is cash/PayPay only.

kyr_kyoto_senmaru_shakariki_.gf_detail: This is a tsukemen and ramen specialist: wheat-flour noodles served with a pork-bone-and-fish (niboshi) double broth and a tare that is virtually always wheat-based soy sauce. There is no indication of any gluten-free noodle, broth, or accommodation, and no dedicated preparation area. Not suitable for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.
kyr_kyoto_senmaru_shakariki_.vegan_detail: The shop is built around an animal-heavy broth (tonkotsu pork bone plus dried-fish niboshi). The signature bowls are all meat/fish based and there is no listed vegetarian or vegan option. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kyr_kyoto_senmaru_shakariki_.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun: 11:00-15:00 (L.O. 14:30) and dinner service in the evening; closed Wednesdays plus occasional irregular closures. Sources differ slightly on evening hours: one lists 17:30-21:00, another lists 18:00-22:00 (L.O. 21:30). Confirm on the day of visit.
kyr_kyoto_senmaru_shakariki_.notes: [Mom & Pop] Opened in 2004 near Senbon-Marutamachi, just northwest of Nijo Castle, Shakariki built its name as one of the early standard-bearers for tsukemen (dipping noodles) in Kyoto, a city long defined by its own back-fat shoyu ramen tradition. It has run in the same neighborhood spot fo

chef_bio.background: Opened in 2004 near Senbon-Marutamachi, just northwest of Nijo Castle, Shakariki built its name as one of the early standard-bearers for tsukemen (dipping noodles) in Kyoto, a city long defined by its own back-fat shoyu ramen tradition. It has run in the same neighborhood spot for over two decades.
chef_bio.philosophy: An obsessive, customize-to-the-bowl approach: rather than one fixed soup, the kitchen offers five broth variations and matches noodle gauge to each, described as a dedication to the single bowl that sets aside pure business calculation.
chef_bio.specialty: The house style is a rich seafood-and-pork double soup: dried sardine (niboshi) aromatics layered over a deep tonkotsu pork-bone base. The flagship is the 濃厚魚介 (rich seafood) tsukemen, served with thick noodles, and the shop deliberately prepares several broth intensities from light to ultra-rich, each matched to a different noodle thickness.

anecdotes.text: Shakariki is credited as a tsukemen pioneer in Kyoto and as a training ground whose lineage includes the Michelin-recognized ramen shop Touhichi (らぁ麺 とうひち) and the related shop Isshoji Boogie, marking it as an influential mentor in the local ramen scene.

The shop draws a notably broad crowd; observers describe not just male regulars but women and even elementary-school children happily slurping the dipping noodles, a sign of how approachable the rich broth is.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Genjitsutouhi documents the 2004 opening near Nijo, Shakariki's status as a Kyoto tsukemen pioneer, its five broths matched to noodle gauges, the niboshi+tonkotsu 濃厚魚介 tsukemen, its mentor lineage to Michelin-recognized らぁ麺とうひち and Isshoji Boogie, and its broad clientele.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: As a tsukemen and ramen shop, the dipping tare is virtually certain to be standard wheat-based Japanese soy sauce, and the noodles are wheat flour; no gluten-free preparation is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The broth is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) and dried-fish (niboshi) double soup; all bowls are animal-based with no listed vegetarian or vegan option, and shared broth/equipment makes cross-contact unavoidable.

cultural_comfort.note: An English menu is available and the counter-style shop is used to a broad, family-friendly clientele, so non-Japanese-speaking visitors should manage comfortably.

kyr_honke_daiichi_asahi_taka.gf_detail: Classic Kyoto chuka-soba: wheat noodles plus a wheat-based raw soy sauce (Fushimi nama-shoyu) tare in a pork-bone broth. No gluten-free noodles or accommodation is mentioned anywhere. Not celiac-safe.
kyr_honke_daiichi_asahi_taka.vegan_detail: There is a "肉なし（野菜入）ラーメン" (no-chashu, vegetable) bowl, but it is still served in the pork-bone (chintan) broth with wheat noodles and wheat soy-sauce tare, so it is neither vegan nor vegetarian. No plant-based broth option exists.
kyr_honke_daiichi_asahi_taka.notes: [Mom & Pop] Honke Daiichi Asahi originated in 1947 (Showa 22). Founder Yuji Taguchi learned ramen-making while helping at the neighboring Shinpuku Saikan (founded 1938), regarded as the source of Kyoto ramen, and first opened the popular eatery 'Asahi Shokudo.' When the ramen he served proved unexpectedly popular, he renamed it 'Daiichi Asahi' in 1956 and converted it into a dedicated ramen shop, which is the start of its present form. The main shop stands in Takabashi, about a 5-minute walk from the Karasuma Central Exit of Kyoto Station.

chef_bio.origin: 京都・下京区／京都駅東（高橋）
chef_bio.background: 本家 第一旭の起こりは1947年（昭和22年）。創業者・田口有司が、京都ラーメンの源流とされる隣の「新福菜館」（1938年創業）を手伝いながらラーメンづくりを学び、まず大衆食堂『旭食堂』を開いた。ところが供したラーメンが思いのほか評判を呼び、1956年に『第一旭』と改名してラーメン専門店へと業態転換したのが現在の姿の始まり。京都駅烏丸中央口から徒歩約5分、高橋（たかばし）の地に本店を構える。
chef_bio.philosophy: 夜明けの最初の光（第一旭）のように京都で輝く一杯を——白濁させない澄んだスープと無添加・素材本位の味を、守り続け磨き続ける。
chef_bio.specialty: 看板は素朴な一杯の「ラーメン」、そして人気の「特製ラーメン」。豚骨を白濁させる前に引き上げて澄ませた清湯（ちんたん）スープに、京都・伏見の無添加生醤油のタレを合わせ、ニンニクや野菜の臭み消しに頼らない澄んだ醤油味に仕立てる。麺は近藤製麺の特注ブレンドの中太ストレート。チャーシューは脂が控えめで旨みの濃い国産雌豚を使い、赤身（赤）か脂身（白）かを無料で指定できる。たっぷりの京都・九条ねぎを惜しみなく盛るのも持ち味。

anecdotes.text: 京都ラーメンの真の源流とされる老舗『新福菜館』（1938年創業）が本店のすぐ隣に並び、二軒は定休日をあえてずらして（第一旭は木曜、新福菜館は水曜）80年近く隣同士で共存してきた。両店をはしごする『たかばしはしご』は地元の楽しみ方として親しまれている。
年間およそ24万人が訪れる京都ラーメンの代表格で、早朝から行列ができることでも知られる。

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: iekei.shop details the 1947 founding by 田口有司, who learned ramen while helping the neighboring 新福菜館 (1938), opened 旭食堂 and renamed it 第一旭 in 1956, plus the staggered Thu/Wed days off and the たかばしはしご custom; PR Times states ~240,000 annual visitors and constant early-morning lines.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water and served in a pork-bone broth seasoned with wheat-based soy-sauce tare — no separation from gluten is possible.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tare uses additive-free raw soy sauce (nama-shoyu) from Fushimi, Kyoto, which is brewed from wheat and soybeans — it contains gluten.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The base broth is pork-bone (chintan) for every bowl, including the no-chashu 'vegetable' ramen, so no bowl is free of animal product.

positives.text: Many free customizations (noodle firmness, broth richness, soy intensity, chashu lean/fatty, extra negi and bean sprouts) let diners adjust a bowl, though none remove the core wheat/pork allergens.

cultural_comfort.note: A famous, perpetually busy Kyoto-Station ramen institution with ticket-machine ordering, shared seating when crowded, and frequent foreign visitors — a friendly konnichiwa and pointing at the menu will carry you through.

kyr_mugi_no_yoake.gf_detail: Not gluten-free or celiac-safe. The whole concept is wheat: custom thin/flat wheat noodles milled from a specific wheat variety, served in a dashi-shoyu broth (soy-sauce tare typically contains wheat). No gluten-free noodle or menu option is offered. Anyone strictly avoiding gluten should not eat here.
kyr_mugi_no_yoake.vegan_detail: Not a vegan or vegetarian place. The signature bowls are built on chicken, pork and seafood dashi (and feature scallop, beef or duck), so the broths and toppings are animal-based. No vegan ramen is advertised.
kyr_mugi_no_yoake.hours_raw: Mon 11:00-14:00; Tue-Fri 11:00-15:00 & 18:00-20:00; Sat 11:00-15:00 & 17:30-20:00; Sun 10:30-14:00. Times listed are open hours; last orders earlier. Hours and closures are irregular — check the shop's SNS before visiting. (Some listings show different/condensed hours, e.g. closed Mondays and Sunday evenings.)
kyr_mugi_no_yoake.notes: [Mom & Pop] The owner-chef is a ramen obsessive who started a ramen-research club while at Doshisha University, then trained at respected shops (including Tsurumusha and Menya Yutaka). Before opening, he went to work for a major flour milling company so he could understand wheat and noodle-m

chef_bio.background: The owner-chef is a ramen obsessive who started a ramen-research club while at Doshisha University, then trained at respected shops (including Tsurumusha and Menya Yutaka). Before opening, he went to work for a major flour milling company so he could understand wheat and noodle-making from the grain up — and that wheat-first knowledge is built into everything the shop serves.
chef_bio.philosophy: Pepper as a Kyoto signature, and wheat treated with a miller's precision: the house noodles are thin and flat, milled from a specific wheat variety, with a smooth, almost inaniwa-udon-like texture meant to match the delicate broth rather than overpower it.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the scallop-and-sansho chuka-soba: a clear, refined dashi-shoyu built from chicken, pork and seafood, finished with the bright, citrus-tingly bite of sansho (Japanese pepper). A beef-shoyu-and-sansho version and a sansho tsukemen round out the core lineup, with seasonal limited bowls (a straw-grilled duck-and-sansho ramen, chilled corn ramen, and a sesame cold tsukemen) appearing through the year.

anecdotes.text: The shop opened February 17, 2022 and earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand almost immediately — less than a year in — with the chef in his twenties, described as the youngest to be recognized in the ramen category in Michelin history.

The straw-grilled duck-and-sansho limited bowl is so sought-after that it can sell out almost as soon as the shop opens — one reviewer heard the 'sold out' call while still waiting to be served; reviewers single out the powerful aroma of the straw-fired duck.
Before opening, the chef worked for a flour milling company to master milling so he could develop the shop's custom thin, flat noodles from a chosen wheat variety.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Genjitsutouhi profiles the chef's Doshisha ramen-club start, training at Tsurumusha and Menya Yutaka, his flour-milling stint and the resulting inaniwa-like thin flat noodles, the Feb-17-2022 opening, the near-immediate Bib Gourmand (youngest in the ramen category in Michelin history), and the fast-selling straw-grilled duck-sansho limited bowl.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The entire kitchen is built around wheat: custom wheat noodles are the centerpiece and are made and handled throughout the space, so flour/gluten cross-contact is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowls are dashi-shoyu (soy-sauce based). Standard ramen soy-sauce tare typically contains wheat, and no wheat-free tare is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths are made from chicken, pork and seafood dashi and bowls feature scallop, beef or duck, so there is no animal-free preparation here.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 9-seat counter ramen-ya run by a serious young chef; little to no English is expected, so a few words of Japanese and following counter etiquette (one bowl per seat) will go a long way.

kyr_gion_duck_noodles.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The house-made noodles are made with German rye and whole-grain (wheat) flour — rye and wheat both contain gluten. The shoyu tare in this style of ramen is almost certainly wheat-based, and no gluten-free menu or accommodation is advertised. People with celiac disease or wheat allergy should avoid.
kyr_gion_duck_noodles.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The entire concept is built on a free-range duck (Kishu/紀州鴨) broth, with duck-meat toppings (loin or thigh) and marinated egg. No plant-based broth or vegan bowl is offered.
kyr_gion_duck_noodles.hours_raw: 11:00–21:30 (last order 21:00), open daily (no regular closing days)
kyr_gion_duck_noodles.notes: [Mom & Pop] A duck-ramen specialist tucked into a narrow Gion back alley a few minutes from Gion-Shijo Station and Yasaka Shrine. It is run by a French-trained chef who brings a fine-dining sensibility to ramen, and is a sister shop to the acclaimed Osaka (Hirakata) noodle bar Menroku (麺麓),

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto (Gion), as a sister location to Osaka's Menroku
chef_bio.background: A duck-ramen specialist tucked into a narrow Gion back alley a few minutes from Gion-Shijo Station and Yasaka Shrine. It is run by a French-trained chef who brings a fine-dining sensibility to ramen, and is a sister shop to the acclaimed Osaka (Hirakata) noodle bar Menroku (麺麓), which opened in December 2018.
chef_bio.philosophy: A 'restaurant-like' (レストランのような) approach to ramen: refined, clean umami over heaviness, an unusually pure duck aroma, and a minimalist identity expressed through an emoji-only sign rather than traditional ramen-shop branding.
chef_bio.specialty: Duck ramen built on a clear, intensely aromatic broth made from branded free-range Kishu duck (紀州鴨) and kombu, served with house-made noodles milled with German rye and whole-grain flour. Diners choose their duck topping — loin (ロース) or thigh (もも) — and there are rich-white-broth tsukemen variations finished with fruit sauces (cherry or mandarin) plus a Western-style duck pilaf.

anecdotes.text: The shop's sign is composed entirely of emoji (a duck and a bowl of ramen) rather than any written name, fitting its understated, fine-dining-inspired identity.
Reviewers single out the broth for a depth of duck aroma rarely found elsewhere — 'the first dish where I felt the fragrance of duck to this degree.'
Organic grape sansho (ブドウ山椒) is offered as a flavor-changer mid-bowl.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyotopi and gcjapan describe the French-trained chef, the sister relationship to Osaka/Hirakata's Menroku (麺麓, Dec 2018), the Kishu-duck + kombu clear broth, German-rye whole-grain noodles, the loin/thigh choice, fruit-sauce tsukemen and Western duck pilaf, the emoji-only sign, and the organic grape-sansho flavor changer.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No ingredient breakdown of the tare/soy sauce is published; standard ramen shoyu tare is wheat-based, so wheat should be assumed present.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: SAFETY DEFECT, and it points the reader at the wrong grain. The claim rests on an assumed wheat shoyu tare while the page — and the shop's own current Tabelog blurb, 「麺は鴨の旨みに負けないよう、ドイツ産ライ麦を使った風味豊かな全粒粉麺を採用」, and a 2026-07-29 Yahoo News piece, 「麺は、ドイツ産ライ麦を使った自家製の全粒粉麺」 — state plainly that the noodles

cultural_comfort.note: English-speaking staff are available and the shop regularly serves international visitors, so foreign diners can order comfortably.

kyr_shinjuku_menya_fuhka.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. This is a classic ramen shop built on hand-kneaded wheat noodles, served in clear salt (shio) broths blending animal and seafood/vegetable stocks. Even the salt-forward bowls rely on wheat noodles, and no gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or allergen accommodation is documented. A diner with celiac disease should not eat here; gluten-avoiders by preference would still be consuming wheat noodles in every bowl.
kyr_shinjuku_menya_fuhka.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The signature broths are built on animal stock (the menu includes charcoal-grilled local-chicken ramen and duck-salt ramen) combined with seafood and vegetable stocks, and bowls are topped with chashu pork. No vegan or vegetarian ramen is offered or documented.
kyr_shinjuku_menya_fuhka.hours_raw: Tabelog lists 11:30–13:50 and 18:00–21:00 daily; some guides list the bands slightly wider (lunch to 14:00, dinner to 22:00). Closures are irregular and announced on the shop's X/Twitter.

chef_bio.background: Born in 1954, Uemura worked for a fish company before moving to Kansai and running several restaurants. He opened Shinjuku Menya Fuhka in Kyoto in 2001 at age 47, at a time when salt ramen was virtually unknown in a city dominated by rich, fatty pork-bone broths — many people warned him the concept would fail. He briefly closed early on to refine his recipe after realizing Kyoto's hot, humid summer (the shop opened in August) shifted customers' taste away from the cold-northern, heavily-salted style he had trained in.
chef_bio.philosophy: Uemura rejects a profit-first approach, saying he doesn't think of ramen as a money-making tool and prioritizing quality over margin. He wants guests to taste attentively — phones and reading are discouraged at the counter, and children under elementary-school age are not admitted because he wants diners with a developed enough palate to appreciate the subtlety of the broth.
chef_bio.specialty: The 天然塩らーめん (natural-salt ramen) is the signature bowl — a clear, golden broth built on a rare cooking technique. Uemura whisks egg whites with salt, heats them and repeatedly skims the surface foam, drawing off harshness until a mild, refined clarity remains, then blends animal and vegetable stocks behind it. He builds the salt itself from Ishigaki Island salt blended with two other salts, and the noodles are kneaded by hand each day. The duck-salt ramen, charcoal-grilled local-chicken ramen, and salt tsukemen round out the menu, and the long-cooked, tender chashu is a frequent favorite.

anecdotes.text: When Uemura opened in 2001, Kyoto ramen meant heavy, fatty pork-bone broth and salt ramen barely existed locally; people told him it would fail, and he briefly closed to re-tune his recipe after learning that Kyoto's humid August climate changed how the broth landed on customers' palates compared with the cold northern region where he trained.
His broth uses an uncommon clarifying technique — egg whites whisked with salt, heated, and repeatedly skimmed until the harsh saltiness is drawn off — to leave a mild, transparent golden soup.
He recalculates his hand-made noodle recipe to the flour and the season's humidity and stays in regular contact with the mill, noting the differences between Kansai and Kanto flour.
Now in his early 70s (born 1954), he has been trying to train a successor since around 2022, though earlier apprentices gave up during the demanding broth-preparation stage.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: k4-media interviews Uemura (b. 1954): ex-fish-company, several Kansai restaurants, opened Fuhka in 2001 at 47 as a Kyoto salt-ramen pioneer; it details the August-opening climate stumble and reformulation, the egg-white salt-clarifying technique, Ishigaki + two salts, daily hand-kneaded noodles, the no-phones/no-young-children counter rules, and the successor search underway since ~2022.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Every bowl is built on hand-kneaded wheat noodles; no gluten-free option or allergen handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Chashu and some bowls carry a soy-sauce element typical of ramen, which is normally wheat-based; no wheat-free tare is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths are animal- and seafood-based (chicken/duck plus seafood and vegetable stocks) and bowls are topped with chashu pork; no separate vegan preparation exists.

cultural_comfort.note: A serious, owner-run counter shop where mindful eating is expected (no reading or phones at the counter, and young children are not admitted); little to no English, so basic Japanese or a guide helps.

kyr_nekomata.gf_detail: Abura soba is built on chewy wheat flat noodles dressed with a soy-based (wheat-containing) tare and sesame oil, so the core dish is not gluten-free. No gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or allergen accommodation is advertised. Not suitable for celiacs.
kyr_nekomata.vegan_detail: This is a meat-and-fish-forward abura soba shop — the soy tare and broth flavorings typically involve animal products, and side dishes include chicken tempura, cutlet skewers and dumplings. No vegan options are advertised. Toppings like chopped onion and green onion exist but the base dish is not vegan.
kyr_nekomata.hours_raw: 10:00–20:30 (L.O. 20:00); closed Sundays. Note: some listings show 11:00–21:00 or daily operation with irregular closures; current Instagram indicates 10:00–20:30, Sunday closed.
kyr_nekomata.notes: [Mom & Pop] ねこまた sits right in the thick of the Kiyomizu tourist district, on the Higashioji/Matsubara-dori approach between the Kiyomizu-yon and Kiyomizu-go intersections at the foot of Kiyomizu-dera. chef_bio.background: ねこまた sits in the thick of the Kiyomizu tourist district, on Matsubara-dori along Higashioji-dori, between the Shijo and Gojo intersections at the foot of the approach to Kiyomizu-dera. It is described as Kansai's first dedicated abura-soba specialty shop, opening before the soupless-noodle craze caught on in the region — which earns it a quiet reputation for the completeness and polish of its bowls. The room is small: roughly eight counter seats plus a few tables, serving both local noodle fans and overseas visitors.
chef_bio.philosophy: A single-minded focus on abura soba — neither ramen nor yakisoba, but its own noodle culture — done simply and well in a small shop.
chef_bio.specialty: Soupless abura soba: thick, flat kishimen-like noodles tossed at the bottom of the bowl with sesame oil and a soy-based tare so the oil, sauce and noodles cling together into a rich, mellow tangle. Three core styles are offered — the soy-based original, a spicy miso (辛味噌), and a shrimp-scented natural-salt version — with menma, diced chashu, negi and narutomaki on top. Complimentary chopped raw onion is added for crunch, and diners thoroughly mix the bowl, then adjust with chili oil and vinegar to taste.

anecdotes.text: Billed as Kansai's first abura-soba specialty shop, started before mazesoba/abura-soba became popular, which is part of why locals praise how dialed-in the bowls are.
Diners are encouraged to load on the complimentary chopped onion and then adjust with chili oil and vinegar, customizing each bowl as they eat.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi (DLt7w) describes ねこまた as 関西初の油そば専門店 on Matsubara-dori (Higashioji) in the Kiyomizu/Shimizu area near Kiyomizu-dera, offering three styles (醤油ベース原型・辛味噌・海老の天然塩), flat kishimen-like noodles with menma/chashu/negi/narutomaki, free 刻み玉ねぎ, and about 8 counter seats plus tables.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The abura soba is dressed with a soy-based tare; standard Japanese soy sauce/tare contains wheat, and the noodles themselves are wheat — no wheat-free tare is advertised.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, casual abura-soba counter shop in a heavy tourist zone near Kiyomizu-dera; a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu will carry you through, though staff are used to international visitors.

kyr_kanton_ryori_hosen.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. The signature karashi-soba (撈麺) is boiled wheat Chinese noodles tossed in mustard-soy sauce, topped with a thickened chicken-bone and kombu broth "an" — wheat noodles plus wheat-based soy sauce. Spring rolls, shumai and fried rice likewise rely on wheat wrappers/seasoning and shared woks. No indication of gluten-free options or accommodation; treat as unsafe for celiac.
kyr_kanton_ryori_hosen.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly kitchen. Kyoto-Chinese cooking here is built on chicken-bone and kombu dashi broths, pork, and shrimp/chicken (the karashi-soba is officially listed as エビカシワソバ — shrimp and chicken). No vegan dishes are indicated.
kyr_kanton_ryori_hosen.hours_raw: Wed–Sun & holidays 11:30–14:30 (last order 14:00) / 17:00–20:00 (last order 19:30). Closed Mon & Tue.

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto, in the lineage of the landmark Kyoto-Chinese restaurant 鳳舞 (Homai)
chef_bio.background: Hosen carries the soul of 鳳舞, the restaurant widely regarded as the source of Kyoto-style Chinese cooking, founded in 1967 by Cantonese chef Kō Kakichi (高華吉), who arrived in Kyoto in the Taisho era and softened bold Cantonese cooking into the subtle, dashi-forward 京風中華 that Kyoto came to love. When 鳳舞 closed in 2009 after a much-mourned run, its kitchen chiefs carried the recipes forward — Hosen was opened that same year by 鳳舞 kitchen chief 福田功雄 (Fukuda Isao) together with 三野真人 (Mino Masato), so the beloved flavor would not be lost.
chef_bio.philosophy: 京風中華 — keeping the refined, lighter, dashi-driven Kyoto interpretation of Cantonese cooking alive exactly as it was passed down from 鳳舞, rather than chasing mainland intensity.
chef_bio.specialty: カラシソバ (karashi-soba), listed on the menu as 撈麺 / エビカシワソバ: boiled wheat Chinese noodles tossed in a mustard-soy sauce and crowned with a glossy 'an' thickened sauce built on chicken-and-kombu broth, with peeled shrimp, chicken, green onion, lettuce and dried shiitake. The mustard — dissolved in Kyoto vinegar rather than water — is the signature, and the kitchen lets you dial it to taste.

anecdotes.text: Hosen was born the same year 鳳舞 closed (2009), opened by 鳳舞's kitchen chief so the beloved Kyoto-Chinese flavor would survive.

The mustard in the karashi-soba is fully adjustable — regulars order it mild, extra-hot, or even as a 'karashi-soba with no karashi (mustard) at all,' and can request omitting shrimp, chicken or scallion.
The karashi-soba style traces to Kō Kakichi (高華吉), a Cantonese chef who opened 鳳舞 in 1967 and reworked his cooking to suit Kyoto's subtle, dashi-forward palate.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Brutus names Hosen's founders as 福田功雄 (鳳舞 kitchen chief) and 三野真人 (opened 2009), and traces 鳳舞 to 高華吉 (Kō Kakichi), a Cantonese chef who founded it in 1967 and lightened his cooking for Kyoto; karashi-soba = 撈麺 with mustard dissolved in Kyoto vinegar, fully adjustable. kyotopi (wP9Ta) confirms Hosen was opened in 2009 by 鳳舞's last kitchen chief preserving the flavor.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The signature dish is wheat Chinese noodles tossed in mustard-soy sauce under a chicken/kombu broth an; spring rolls, shumai and fried rice are cooked in shared woks — gluten is pervasive throughout the menu.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The karashi-soba is dressed in カラシ醤油 (mustard soy sauce); standard Japanese/Chinese soy sauce is wheat-based.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths are made from chicken bone and kombu, and the signature noodle is shrimp-and-chicken (エビカシワソバ); no plant-only preparations indicated.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The kitchen will adjust the amount of mustard to order, including making the dish with no mustard at all — showing willingness to customize, though this is a seasoning preference and not an allergen-handling policy.
staff_allergy_handling.source_wording: 「カラシの量を自由に注文できるのは〈鳳泉〉。…「カラシ抜きのカラシソバを頼む方も」」 AND, in the same Information block, 「カラシ多め・少なめ、エビ抜き、カシワ抜き、ネギ抜きなどにも対応可。」

cultural_comfort.note: A beloved, busy local Kyoto-Chinese counter-and-table spot where the owner is known as warm and easygoing; a few words of Japanese and patience at peak lunch/dinner go a long way, and cash is essential.

kyr_ramen_sen_no_kaze_shijo_.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The ramen and tsukemen use wheat noodles, the broth is pork-bone (tonkotsu) based, and a shoyu (soy sauce, normally wheat-containing) tare is used for the 京の醤油 bowl. No gluten-free noodles, tare, or preparation is offered, and there is no information indicating any allergen accommodation. Not suitable for celiacs.
kyr_ramen_sen_no_kaze_shijo_.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The broth is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) base and the bowls are topped with grilled chashu pork; signature items are meat-based. No vegetable/vegan ramen option was found.
kyr_ramen_sen_no_kaze_shijo_.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, long-running ramen counter tucked into the Shinkyogoku covered arcade just off Shijo-Kawaramachi, open for roughly fifteen years and a familiar fixture in one of central Kyoto's busiest shopping streets.

chef_bio.background: A small ramen counter tucked into the Shinkyogoku covered arcade just off Shijo-Kawaramachi, open since June 2010 — roughly fifteen years — and a familiar fixture a minute's walk from Kawaramachi Station in one of central Kyoto's busiest shopping streets.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen aims for a refined, easy-drinking bowl: richness without heaviness, so the soup stays pleasant from first spoonful to last.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the 京の塩 (Kyo-no-shio, Kyoto salt ramen): a broth that is creamy in body yet surprisingly light and clean to the last sip, topped with chashu pork. A 京の醤油 (Kyoto soy sauce) version and tsukemen dipping noodles round out the menu, with gyoza on the side.

anecdotes.text: The little Japanese-fronted shop has become a hit with overseas visitors and often has a queue of around thirty minutes at lunch.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog lists らーめん千の風 四条河原町店 as opened 2010-06-24 in the Shinkyogoku arcade (中之町580), a 15-seat counter/table shop about 1 min from Kawaramachi Station, signature 京の塩. Retty describes the 京の塩 as a creamy-yet-surprisingly-light broth, praised by overseas guests, with roughly 30-minute lunch queues.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The 京の醤油 (Kyoto soy sauce) ramen is built on a soy-sauce tare, which in standard Japanese ramen contains wheat.

cultural_comfort.note: A compact, tourist-friendly counter shop in the busy Shinkyogoku arcade that regularly draws international visitors, so a friendly konnichiwa and pointing at the menu will get you through fine.
